entries.63dc85e3aa225702a46704a0bc3391f2a68cdf25: <div sID="gen7022" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="22" osisID="1Kgs.22" sID="1Kgs.22"/> <div eID="gen7022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7023" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7024" type="x-p"/> This chapter finishes the history of Ahab's reign. It was promised in the close of the foregoing chapter that the ruin of his house should not come in his days, but his days were soon at an end. His war with the Syrians at Ramoth-Gilead is that which we have an account of in this chapter. I. His preparations for that war. He consulted, 1. His privy-council, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.1-1Kgs.22.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. 2. Jehoshaphat, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.4">ver. 4</reference>. 3. His prophets. (1.) His own, who encouraged him to go on this expedition (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.5-1Kgs.22.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>), Zedekiah particularly, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.11-1Kgs.22.12">ver. 11, 12</reference>. (2.) A prophet of the Lord, Micaiah, who was desired to come by Jehoshaphat (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.7-1Kgs.22.8">ver. 7, 8</reference>), sent for (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.9-1Kgs.22.14">ver. 9, 10-13, 14</reference>), upbraided Ahab with his confidence in the false prophets (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.15">v. 15</reference>), but foretold his fall in this expedition (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.16-1Kgs.22.18">ver. 16-18</reference>), and gave him an account how he came to be thus imposed upon by his prophets, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.19-1Kgs.22.23">ver. 19-23</reference>. He is abused by Zedekiah (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.24-1Kgs.22.25">ver. 24, 25</reference>), and imprisoned by Ahab, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.26-1Kgs.22.28">ver. 26-28</reference>. II. The battle itself, in which, 1. Jehoshaphat is exposed. But, 2. Ahab is slain, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.29-1Kgs.22.40">ver. 29-40</reference>. In the close of the chapter we have a short account, (1.) Of the good reign of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.41-1Kgs.22.50">ver. 41-50</reference>. (2.) Of the wicked reign of Ahaziah king of Israel, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.51-1Kgs.22.53">ver. 51-53</reference>.
entries.9a243c8e3339b397aa059b096a91d4a456a39e9b: <div eID="gen7024" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7023" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Jehoshaphat's League with Ahab. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 897.)</title> <div sID="gen7025" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And they continued three years without war between Syria and Israel. <hi type="super">2</hi> And it came to pass in the third year, that Jehoshaphat the king of Judah came down to the king of Israel. <hi type="super">3</hi> And the king of Israel said unto his servants, Know ye that Ramoth in Gilead <hi type="italic">is</hi> ours, and we <hi type="italic">be</hi> still, <hi type="italic">and</hi> take it not out of the hand of the king of Syria? <hi type="super">4</hi> And he said unto Jehoshaphat, Wilt thou go with me to battle to Ramoth-gilead? And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> as thou <hi type="italic">art,</hi> my people as thy people, my horses as thy horses. <hi type="super">5</hi> And Jehoshaphat said unto the king of Israel, Enquire, I pray thee, at the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> to day. <hi type="super">6</hi> Then the king of Israel gathered the prophets together, about four hundred men, and said unto them, Shall I go against Ramoth-gilead to battle, or shall I forbear? And they said, Go up; for the Lord shall deliver <hi type="italic">it</hi> into the hand of the king. <hi type="super">7</hi> And Jehoshaphat said, <hi type="italic">Is there</hi> not here a prophet of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> besides, that we might enquire of him? <hi type="super">8</hi> And the king of Israel said unto Jehoshaphat, <hi type="italic">There is</hi> yet one man, Micaiah the son of Imlah, by whom we may enquire of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : but I hate him; for he doth not prophesy good concerning me, but evil. And Jehoshaphat said, Let not the king say so. <hi type="super">9</hi> Then the king of Israel called an officer, and said, Hasten <hi type="italic">hither</hi> Micaiah the son of Imlah. <hi type="super">10</hi> And the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah sat each on his throne, having put on their robes, in a void place in the entrance of the gate of Samaria; and all the prophets prophesied before them. <hi type="super">11</hi> And Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made him horns of iron: and he said, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , With these shalt thou push the Syrians, until thou have consumed them. <hi type="super">12</hi> And all the prophets prophesied so, saying, Go up to Ramoth-gilead, and prosper: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall deliver <hi type="italic">it</hi> into the king's hand. <hi type="super">13</hi> And the messenger that was gone to call Micaiah spake unto him, saying, Behold now, the words of the prophets <hi type="italic">declare</hi> good unto the king with one mouth: let thy word, I pray thee, be like the word of one of them, and speak <hi type="italic">that which is</hi> good. <hi type="super">14</hi> And Micaiah said, <hi type="italic">As</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth, what the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> saith unto me, that will I speak. <div eID="gen7025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7026" type="x-p"/> Though Ahab continued under guilt and wrath, and the dominion of the lusts to which he had sold himself, yet, as a reward for his professions of repentance and humiliation, though the time drew near when he should descend into battle and perish, yet we have him blessed with a three years' peace (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.1">v. 1</reference>) and an honourable visit made him by Jehoshaphat king of Judah, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.2">v. 2</reference>. The Jews have a fabulous conceit, that when Ahab humbled himself for his sin, and lay in sackcloth, he sent for Jehoshaphat to come to him, to chastise him; and that he staid with him for some time, and gave him so many stripes every day. This is a groundless tradition. He came now, it is probable, to consult him about the affairs of their kingdoms. It is strange that so great a man as Jehoshaphat would pay so much respect to a kingdom revolted from the house of David, and that so good a man should show so much kindness to a king revolted from the worship of God. But, though he was a godly man, his temper was too easy, which betrayed him into snares and inconveniences. The Syrians durst not give Ahab any disturbance. But, <div eID="gen7026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7027" type="x-p"/> I. Ahab here meditates a war against the Syrians, and advises concerning it with those about him, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.3">v. 3</reference>. The king of Syria gave him the provocation; when he lay at his mercy, he promised to restore him his cities (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.34">ch. xx. 34</reference>), and Ahab foolishly took his word, when he ought not to have dismissed him till the cities were put into his possession. But now he knows by experience, what he ought before to have considered, that as the kisses, so the promises, <hi type="italic">of an enemy are deceitful,</hi> and there is no confidence to be put in leagues extorted by distress. Benhadad is one of those princes that think themselves bound by their word no further and no longer than it is for their interest. Whether any other cities were restored we do not find, but Ramoth-Gilead was not, a considerable city in the tribe of Gad, on the other side Jordan, a Levites' city, and one of the cities of refuge. Ahab blames himself, and his people, that they did not bestir themselves to recover it out of the hands of the Syrians, and to chastise Ben-hadad's violation of his league; and resolves to let that ungrateful perfidious prince know that as he had given him peace he could give him trouble. Ahab has a good cause, yet succeeds not. Equity is not to be judged of by prosperity. <div eID="gen7027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7028" type="x-p"/> II. He engages Jehoshaphat, and draws him in, to join with him in this expedition, for the recovery of Ramoth-Gilead, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.4">v. 4</reference>. And here I do not wonder that Ahab should desire the assistance of so pious and prosperous a neighbour. Even bad men have often coveted the friendship of the good. It is desirable to have an interest in those that have an interest in heaven, and to have those with us that have God with them. But it is strange that Jehoshaphat will go so entirely into Ahab's interests as to say, <hi type="italic">I am as thou art, and my people as thy people.</hi> I hope not; Jehoshaphat and his people are not so wicked and corrupt as Ahab and his people. Too great a complaisance to evildoers has brought many good people, through unwariness, into a dangerous fellowship with <hi type="italic">the unfruitful works of darkness.</hi> Jehoshaphat had like to have paid dearly for his compliment when, in battle, he was taken for Ahab. Yet some observe that in joining with Israel against Syria he atoned for his father's fault in joining with Syria against Israel, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.19-1Kgs.15.20">ch. xv. 19, 20</reference>. <div eID="gen7028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7029" type="x-p"/> III. At the special instance and request of Jehoshaphat, he asks counsel of the prophets concerning this expedition. Ahab thought it enough to consult with his statesmen, but Jehoshaphat moves that they should <hi type="italic">enquire of the word of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.5">v. 5</reference>. Note, 1. Whithersoever a good man goes he desires to take God along with him, and will acknowledge him in all his ways, ask leave of him, and look up to him for success. 2. Whithersoever a good man goes he ought to take his religion along with him, and not be ashamed to own it, no, not when he is with those who have no kindness for it. Jehoshaphat has not left behind him, at Jerusalem, his affection, his veneration, for <hi type="italic">the word of the Lord,</hi> but both avows it and endeavours to introduce it into Ahab's court. If Ahab drew him into his wars, he will draw Ahab into his devotions. <div eID="gen7029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7030" type="x-p"/> IV. Ahab's 400 prophets, the standing regiment he had of them (<hi type="italic">prophets of the groves</hi> they called them), agreed to encourage him in this expedition and to assure him of success, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.6">v. 6</reference>. He put the question to them with a seeming fairness: <hi type="italic">Shall I go or shall I forbear?</hi> But they knew which way his inclination was and designed only to humour the two kings. To please Jehoshaphat, they made use of the name <hi type="italic">Jehovah:</hi> He shall <hi type="italic">deliver it into the hand of the king;</hi> they stole the word from the true prophets (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.30">Jer. xxiii. 30</reference>) and spoke their language. To please Ahab they said, <hi type="italic">Go up.</hi> They had indeed probabilities on their side: Ahab had, not long since, beaten the Syrians twice; he had now a good cause, and was much strengthened by his alliance with Jehoshaphat. But they pretended to speak by prophecy, not by rational conjecture, by divine, not human, foresight: "Thou shalt certainly recover Ramoth-Gilead." Zedekiah, a leading man among these prophets, in imitation of the true prophets, illustrated his false prophecy with a sign, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.11">v. 11</reference>. He made himself a pair of iron horns, representing the two kings, and their honour and power (both of which were signified by horns, exaltation and force), and with these the Syrians must be pushed. All the prophets agreed, as one man, that Ahab should return from this expedition a conqueror, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.12">v. 12</reference>. Unity is not always the mark of a true church and a true ministry. Here were 400 men that prophesied with one mind and one mouth, and yet all in an error. <div eID="gen7030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7031" type="x-p"/> V. Jehoshaphat cannot relish this sort of preaching; it is not like what he was used to. The false prophets cannot so mimic the true but that he who had spiritual senses exercised could discern the fallacy, and therefore he enquired for a <hi type="italic">prophet of the Lord besides,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.7">v. 7</reference>. He is too much of a courtier to say any thing by way of reflection on the king's chaplains, but he waits to see a <hi type="italic">prophet of the Lord,</hi> intimating that he could not look upon these to be so. They <hi type="italic">seemed to be somewhat</hi> (whatever they were, it made no matter to him), but, in conference, they <hi type="italic">added nothing to him,</hi> they gave him no satisfaction, <reference osisRef="Gal.2.6">Gal. ii. 6</reference>. One faithful prophet of the Lord was worth them all. <div eID="gen7031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7032" type="x-p"/> VI. Ahab has another, but one he hates, Micaiah by name, and, to please Jehoshaphat, he is willing to have him sent for, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.8-1Kgs.22.10">v. 8-10</reference>. Ahab owned that they might <hi type="italic">enquire of the Lord by him,</hi> that he was a true prophet, and one that knew God's mind. And yet, 1. He hated him, and was not ashamed to own to the king of Judah that he did so, and to give this for a reason. He <hi type="italic">doth not prophesy good concerning me, but evil.</hi> And whose fault was that? If Ahab had done well, he would have heard nothing but good from heaven; if he do ill, he may thank himself for all the uneasiness which the reproofs and threats of God's word gave him. Note, Those are wretchedly hardened in sin, and are ripening apace for ruin, who hate God's ministers because they deal plainly with them and faithfully warn them of their misery and danger by reason of sin, and reckon those their enemies that <hi type="italic">tell them the truth.</hi> 2. He had (it should seem) imprisoned him; for, when he committed him (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.26">v. 26</reference>), he bade the officer carry him back, namely, to the place whence he came. We may suppose that this was he that reproved him for his clemency to Ben-hadad (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.38-1Kgs.20.43">ch. xx. 38</reference>, &c.) and for so doing was cast into prison, where he had lain these three years. This was the reason why Ahab knew where to find him so readily, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.9">v. 9</reference>. But his imprisonment had not excluded him for divine visits: the spirit of prophecy continued with him there. He was bound, but <hi type="italic">the word of the Lord was not.</hi> Nor did it in the lease abate his courage, nor make him less confident or faithful in delivering his message. Jehoshaphat gave too gentle a reproof to Ahab for expressing his indignation against a faithful prophet: <hi type="italic">Let not the king say so,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.8">v. 8</reference>. He should have said, "Thou art unjust to the prophet, unkind to thyself, and puttest an affront upon his Lord and thine, in saying so." Such sinners as Ahab must be rebuked sharply. However he so far yielded to the reproof that, for fear of provoking Jehoshaphat to break off from his alliance with him, he orders Micaiah to be sent for with all speed, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.9">v. 9</reference>. The two kings sat each in their robes and chairs of state, in the gate of Samaria, ready to receive this poor prophet, and to hear what he had to say; for many will give God's word the hearing that will not lend it an obedient ear. They were attended with a crowd of flattering prophets, that could not think of prophesying any thing but what was very sweet and very smooth to two such glorious princes now in confederacy. Those that love to be flattered shall not want flatterers. <div eID="gen7032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7033" type="x-p"/> VII. Micaiah is pressed by the officer that fetches him to follow the cry, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.13">v. 13</reference>. That officer was unworthy the name of an Israelite who pretended to prescribe to a prophet; but he thought him altogether such a one as the rest, who studied to please men and not God. He told Micaiah how unanimous the other prophets were in foretelling the king's good success, how agreeable it was to the king, intimating that it was his interest to say as they said—he might thereby gain, not only enlargement, but preferment. Those that dote upon worldly things themselves think every body else should do so too, and true or false, right or wrong, speak and act for their secular interest only. He intimated likewise that it would be to no purpose to contradict such a numerous and unanimous vote; he would be ridiculed, as affecting a foolish singularity, if he should. But Micaiah, who knows better things, protests, and backs his protestation with an oath, that he will deliver his message from God with all faithfulness, whether it be pleasing or displeasing to his prince (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.14">v. 14</reference>): "<hi type="italic">What the Lord saith to me, that will I speak,</hi> without addition, diminution, or alteration." This was nobly resolved, and as became one who had his eye to a greater King than either of these, arrayed with brighter robes, and sitting on a higher throne.
entries.7ba94ea574287de84c2a69e9a24ed82edac19206: <div eID="gen7033" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Micaiah's Prediction. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 897.)</title> <div sID="gen7034" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> So he came to the king. And the king said unto him, Micaiah, shall we go against Ramoth-gilead to battle, or shall we forbear? And he answered him, Go, and prosper: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall deliver <hi type="italic">it</hi> into the hand of the king. <hi type="super">16</hi> And the king said unto him, How many times shall I adjure thee that thou tell me nothing but <hi type="italic">that which is</hi> true in the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ? <hi type="super">17</hi> And he said, I saw all Israel scattered upon the hills, as sheep that have not a shepherd: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said, These have no master: let them return every man to his house in peace. <hi type="super">18</hi> And the king of Israel said unto Jehoshaphat, Did I not tell thee that he would prophesy no good concerning me, but evil? <hi type="super">19</hi> And he said, Hear thou therefore the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : I saw the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left. <hi type="super">20</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said, Who shall persuade Ahab, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead? And one said on this manner, and another said on that manner. <hi type="super">21</hi> And there came forth a spirit, and stood before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and said, I will persuade him. <hi type="super">22</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto him, Wherewith? And he said, I will go forth, and I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets. And he said, Thou shalt persuade <hi type="italic">him,</hi> and prevail also: go forth, and do so. <hi type="super">23</hi> Now therefore, behold, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these thy prophets, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath spoken evil concerning thee. <hi type="super">24</hi> But Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah went near, and smote Micaiah on the cheek, and said, Which way went the Spirit of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> from me to speak unto thee? <hi type="super">25</hi> And Micaiah said, Behold, thou shalt see in that day, when thou shalt go into an inner chamber to hide thyself. <hi type="super">26</hi> And the king of Israel said, Take Micaiah, and carry him back unto Amon the governor of the city, and to Joash the king's son; <hi type="super">27</hi> And say, Thus saith the king, Put this <hi type="italic">fellow</hi> in the prison, and feed him with bread of affliction and with water of affliction, until I come in peace. <hi type="super">28</hi> And Micaiah said, If thou return at all in peace, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath not spoken by me. And he said, Hearken, O people, every one of you. <div eID="gen7034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7035" type="x-p"/> Here Micaiah does well, but, as is common, suffers ill for so doing. <div eID="gen7035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7036" type="x-p"/> I. We are told how faithfully he delivered his message, as one that was more solicitous to please God than to humour either the great or the many. In three ways he delivers his message, and all displeasing to Ahab:— <div eID="gen7036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7037" type="x-p"/> 1. He spoke as the rest of the prophets had spoken, but ironically: <hi type="italic">Go, and prosper,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.15">v. 15</reference>. Ahab put the same question to him that he had put to his own prophets (<hi type="italic">Shall we go, or shall we forbear?</hi>) seeming desirous to know God's mind, when, like Balaam, he was strongly bent to do his own, which Micaiah plainly took notice of when he bade him go, but with such an air and pronunciation as plainly showed he spoke it by way of derision; as if he had said, "I know you are determined to go, and I hear your own prophets are unanimous in assuring you of success; go then and take what follows. They say, <hi type="italic">The Lord shall deliver it into the hand of the king;</hi> but I do not tell thee that <hi type="italic">thus saith the Lord;</hi> no, he saith otherwise." Note, Those deserve to be bantered that love to be flattered; and it is just with God to give up those to their own counsels that give up themselves to their own lusts. <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.9">Eccl. xi. 9</reference>. In answer to this Ahab adjured him to tell him the truth, and not to jest with him (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.16">v. 16</reference>), as if he sincerely desired to know both what God would have him to do and what he would do with him, yet intending to represent the prophet as a perverse ill-humoured man, that would not tell him the truth till he was thus put to his oath, or adjured to do it. <div eID="gen7037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7038" type="x-p"/> 2. Being thus pressed, he plainly foretold that the king would be cut off in this expedition, and his army scattered, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.17">v. 17</reference>. He saw them in a vision, or in a dream, dispersed upon the mountains, as sheep that had no one to guide them. <hi type="italic">Smite the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.13.7">Zech. xiii. 7</reference>. This intimates, (1.) That Israel should be deprived of their king, who was their shepherd. God took notice of it, <hi type="italic">These have no master.</hi> (2.) That they would be obliged to retire <hi type="italic">re infecta—without accomplishing their object.</hi> He does not foresee any great slaughter in the army, but that they should make a dishonorable retreat. <hi type="italic">Let them return every man to his house in peace,</hi> put into disorder indeed for the present, but no great losers by the death of their king; he shall fall in war, but they shall go home in peace. Thus Micaiah, in his prophecy, testified what he had seen and heard (let them take it how they pleased), while the others prophesied merely <hi type="italic">out of their own hearts;</hi> see <reference osisRef="Jer.23.28">Jer. xxiii. 28</reference>. "The prophet that has a dream let him tell that, and so quote his authority; <hi type="italic">and he that has my word, let him speak my word faithfully,</hi> and not his own; for <hi type="italic">what is the chaff to the wheat?</hi>" Now Ahab finds himself aggrieved, turns to Jehoshaphat, and appeals to him whether Micaiah had not manifestly a spite against him, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.18">v. 18</reference>. Those that bear malice to others are generally willing to believe that others bear malice to them, though they have no cause for it, and therefore to put the worst constructions upon all they say. What evil did Micaiah prophesy to Ahab in telling him that, if he proceeded in this expedition, it would be fatal to him, while he might choose whether he would proceed in it or no? The greatest kindness we can do to one that is going a dangerous way is to tell him of his danger. <div eID="gen7038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7039" type="x-p"/> 3. He informed the king how it was that all his prophets encouraged him to proceed, that God permitted Satan by them to deceive him into his ruin, and he by vision knew of it; it was represented to him, and he represented it to Ahab, that the God of heaven had determined he should fall at Ramoth-Gilead (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.19-1Kgs.22.20">v. 19, 20</reference>), that the favour he had wickedly shown to Ben-hadad might be punished by him and his Syrians, and that he being in some doubt whether he should go to Ramoth-Gilead or no, and resolving to be advised by his prophets, they should persuade him to it and prevail (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.21-1Kgs.22.22">v. 21, 22</reference>); and hence it was that they encouraged him with so much assurance (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.23">v. 23</reference>); it was a lie from the father of lies, but by divine permission. This matter is here represented after the manner of men. We are not to imagine that God is ever put upon new counsels, or is ever at a loss for means whereby to effect his purposes, nor that he needs to consult with angels, or any creature, about the methods he should take, nor that he is the author of sin or the cause of any man's either telling or believing a lie; but, besides what was intended by this with reference to Ahab himself, it is to teach us, (1.) That God is a great king above all kings, and has a throne above all the thrones of earthly princes. "You have your thrones," said Micaiah to these two kings, "and you think you may do what you will, and we must all say as you would have us; but <hi type="italic">I saw the Lord sitting upon his throne,</hi> and every man's judgment proceeding from him, and therefore I must say as he says; he is not a man, as you are." (2.) That he is continually attended and served by an innumerable company of angels, those heavenly hosts, who stand by him, ready to go where he sends them and to do what he bids them, messengers of mercy <hi type="italic">on his right hand,</hi> of wrath <hi type="italic">on his left hand.</hi> (3.) That he not only takes cognizance of, but presides over, all the affairs of this lower world, and overrules them <hi type="italic">according to the counsel of his own will.</hi> The rise and fall of princes, the issues of war, and all the great affairs of state, which are the subject of the consultations of wise and great men, are no more above God's direction than the meanest concerns of the poorest cottages are below his notice. (4.) That God has many ways of bringing about his own counsels, particularly concerning the fall of sinners when they are ripe for ruin; he can do it either in this manner or in that manner. (5.) That there are malicious and lying spirits which go about continually seeking to devour, and, in order to that, seeking to deceive, and especially to put lies into the mouths of prophets, by them to entice many to their destruction. (6.) It is not without the divine permission that the devil deceives men, and even thereby God serves his own purposes. <hi type="italic">With him are strength and wisdom, the deceived and the deceivers are his,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.12.16">Job xii. 16</reference>. When he pleases, for the punishment of those who receive not the truth in the love of it, he not only <hi type="italic">lets Satan loose to deceive them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.7-Rev.20.8">Rev. xx. 7, 8</reference>), but <hi type="italic">gives men up to strong delusions to believe</hi> him, <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.11-2Thess.2.12">2 Thess. ii. 11, 12</reference>. (7.) Those are manifestly marked for ruin that are thus given up. God has certainly <hi type="italic">spoken evil concerning those</hi> whom he had given up to be imposed upon by lying prophets. Thus Micaiah gave Ahab fair warning, not only of the danger of proceeding in this war, but of the danger of believing those that encouraged him to proceed. Thus we are warned to <hi type="italic">beware of false prophets,</hi> and to try the spirits; the lying spirit never deceives so fatally as <hi type="italic">in the mouth of prophets.</hi> <div eID="gen7039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7040" type="x-p"/> II. We are told how he was abused for delivering his message thus faithfully, thus plainly, in a way so very proper both to convince and to affect. 1. Zedekiah, a wicked prophet, impudently insulted him in the face of the court, <hi type="italic">smote him on the cheek,</hi> to reproach him, to silence him and stop his mouth, and to express his indignation at him (thus was our blessed Saviour abused, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.67">Matt. xxvi. 67</reference>, that Judge of Israel, <reference osisRef="Mic.5.1">Mic. v. 1</reference>); and as if he not only had the spirit of the Lord, but the monopoly of this Spirit, that he might not go without his leave, he asks, <hi type="italic">Which way went the Spirit of the Lord from me to speak to thee?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.24">v. 24</reference>. The false prophets were always the worst enemies the true prophets had, and not only stirred up the government against them, but were themselves abusive to them, as Zedekiah here. To strike within the verge of the court, especially in the king's presence, is looked upon by our law as a high misdemeanour; yet this wicked prophet gives this abuse to a prophet of the Lord, and is not reprimanded nor bound to his good behaviour for it. Ahab was pleased with it, and Jehoshaphat had not courage to appear for the injured prophet, pretending it was out of his jurisdiction; but Micaiah, though he returns not his blow (God's prophets are not strikers nor persecutors, dare not avenge themselves, render blow for blow, or be in any way accessory to the breach of the peace), yet, since he boasted so much of the Spirit, as those commonly do that know least of his operations, he leaves him to be convinced of his error by the event: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt know when thou hidest thyself in an inner chamber,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.25">v. 25</reference>. It is likely Zedekiah went with Ahab to the battle, and took his horns of iron with him to encourage the soldiers, to see with pleasure the accomplishment of his prophecy, and return in triumph with the king; but, the army being routed, he fled among the rest from the sword of the enemy, sheltered himself as Ben-hadad had done in <hi type="italic">a chamber within a chamber</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.30">ch. xx. 30</reference>), lest he should perish, as he knew he deserved to do, with those whom he had deluded, as Balaam did (<reference osisRef="Num.31.8">Num. xxxi. 8</reference>), and lest the blind prophet should <hi type="italic">fall into the ditch</hi> with the blinded prince whom he had misled. Note, Those that will not have their mistakes rectified in time by the word of God will be undeceived, when it is too late, by the judgments of God. 2. Ahab, that wicked king, committed him to prison (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.27">v. 27</reference>), not only ordered him to be taken into custody, or remitted to the prison whence he came, but to be fed with bread and water, coarse bread and puddle-water, till he should return, not doubting but that he should return a conqueror, and then he would put him to death for a false prophet (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.27">v. 27</reference>)—hard usage for one that would have prevented his ruin! But by this it appeared that God had <hi type="italic">determined to destroy him,</hi> as <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.16">2 Chron. xxv. 16</reference>. How confident is Ahab of success. He doubts not but he shall return in peace, forgetting what he himself had reminded Ben-hadad of, <hi type="italic">Let not him that girdeth on the harness boast;</hi> but there was little likelihood of his coming home in peace when he left one of God's prophets behind him in prison. Micaiah put it upon the issue, and called all the people to be witnesses that he did so: "<hi type="italic">If thou return in peace, the Lord has not spoken by me,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.28">v. 28</reference>. Let me incur the reproach and punishment of a false prophet, if the king come home alive." He ran no hazard by this appeal, for he knew whom he had believed; he that is terrible to the kings of the earth, and treads upon princes as mortar, will rather let thousands of them fall to the ground than one jot or tittle of his own word; he will not fail to <hi type="italic">confirm the word of his servants,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.26">Isa. xliv. 26</reference>.
entries.1fa00e6aa6c9df46c961f959c7a618cbd2139b32: <div eID="gen7040" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Ahab's Death. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 897.)</title> <div sID="gen7041" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead. <hi type="super">30</hi> And the king of Israel said unto Jehoshaphat, I will disguise myself, and enter into the battle; but put thou on thy robes. And the king of Israel disguised himself, and went into the battle. <hi type="super">31</hi> But the king of Syria commanded his thirty and two captains that had rule over his chariots, saying, Fight neither with small nor great, save only with the king of Israel. <hi type="super">32</hi> And it came to pass, when the captains of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat, that they said, Surely it <hi type="italic">is</hi> the king of Israel. And they turned aside to fight against him: and Jehoshaphat cried out. <hi type="super">33</hi> And it came to pass, when the captains of the chariots perceived that it <hi type="italic">was</hi> not the king of Israel, that they turned back from pursuing him. <hi type="super">34</hi> And a <hi type="italic">certain</hi> man drew a bow at a venture, and smote the king of Israel between the joints of the harness: wherefore he said unto the driver of his chariot, Turn thine hand, and carry me out of the host; for I am wounded. <hi type="super">35</hi> And the battle increased that day: and the king was stayed up in his chariot against the Syrians, and died at even: and the blood ran out of the wound into the midst of the chariot. <hi type="super">36</hi> And there went a proclamation throughout the host about the going down of the sun, saying, Every man to his city, and every man to his own country. <hi type="super">37</hi> So the king died, and was brought to Samaria; and they buried the king in Samaria. <hi type="super">38</hi> And <hi type="italic">one</hi> washed the chariot in the pool of Samaria; and the dogs licked up his blood; and they washed his armour; according unto the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> which he spake. <hi type="super">39</hi> Now the rest of the acts of Ahab, and all that he did, and the ivory house which he made, and all the cities that he built, <hi type="italic">are</hi> they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel? <hi type="super">40</hi> So Ahab slept with his fathers; and Ahaziah his son reigned in his stead. <div eID="gen7041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7042" type="x-p"/> The matter in contest between God's prophet and Ahab's prophets is here soon determined, and it is made to appear which was in the right. Here, <div eID="gen7042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7043" type="x-p"/> I. The two kings march with their forces to Ramoth-Gilead, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.29">v. 29</reference>. That the king of Israel, who hated God's prophet, should so far disbelieve his admonition as to persist in his resolution, notwithstanding, is not strange; but that Jehoshaphat, that pious prince, who had desired to enquire by a <hi type="italic">prophet of the Lord,</hi> as disrelishing and discrediting Ahab's prophets, should yet proceed, after so fair a warning, is matter of astonishment. But by the easiness of his temper he was carried away with the delusion (as Barnabas was with the dissimulation, <reference osisRef="Gal.2.13">Gal. ii. 13</reference>) of his friends. He gave too much heed to Ahab's prophets, because they pretended to speak from God too, and in his country he had never been imposed upon by such cheats. He was ready to give his opinion with the majority, and to conclude that it was 400 to one but they should succeed. Micaiah had not forbidden them to go; nay, at first, he said, <hi type="italic">Go, and prosper.</hi> If it came to the worst, it was only Ahab's fall that was foretold, and therefore Jehoshaphat hoped he might safely venture. <div eID="gen7043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7044" type="x-p"/> II. Ahab adopts a contrivance by which he hopes to secure himself and expose his friend (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.30">v. 30</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will disguise myself,</hi> and go in the habit of a common soldier, but let <hi type="italic">Jehoshaphat put on his robes,</hi> to appear in the dress of a general." He pretended thereby to do honour to Jehoshaphat, and to compliment him with the sole command of the army in this action. He shall direct and give orders, and Ahab will serve as a soldier under him. But he intended, 1. To make a liar of a good prophet. Thus he hoped to elude the danger, and so to defeat the threatening, as if, by disguising himself, he could escape the divine cognizance and the judgments that pursued him. 2. To make a fool of a good king, whom he did not cordially love, because he was one that adhered to God and so condemned his apostasy. He knew that if any perished it must be the shepherd (so Micaiah had foretold); and perhaps he had intimation of the charge the enemy had to fight chiefly <hi type="italic">against the king of Israel,</hi> and therefore basely intended to betray Jehoshaphat to the danger, that he might secure himself. Ahab was marked for ruin; one would not have been in his coat for a great sum; yet he will over-persuade this godly king to muster for him. See what those get that join in affinity with vicious men, whose consciences are debauched, and who are lost to every thing that is honourable. How can it be expected that he should be true to his friend that has been false to his God? <div eID="gen7044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7045" type="x-p"/> III. Jehoshaphat, having more piety than policy, put himself into the post of honour, though it was the post of danger, and was thereby brought into the peril of his life, but God graciously delivered him. The king of Syria charged his captains to level their force, not against the king of Judah, for with him he had no quarrel, but against the king of Israel only (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.31">v. 31</reference>), to aim at his person, as if against him he had a particular enmity. Now Ahab was justly repaid for sparing Ben-hadad, who, as the seed of the serpent commonly do, stung the bosom in which he was fostered and saved from perishing. Some think that he designed only to have him taken prisoner, that he might now give him as honourable a treatment as he had formerly received from him. Whatever was the reason, this charge the officers received, and endeavoured to oblige their prince in this matter; for, seeing Jehoshaphat in his royal habit, they took him for the king of Israel, and surrounded him. Now, 1. By his danger God let him know that he was displeased with him for joining in confederacy with Ahab. Jehoshaphat had said, in compliment to Ahab (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.4">v. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">I am as thou art;</hi> and now he was indeed taken for him. Those that associate with evil doers are in danger of sharing in their plagues. 2. By his deliverance God let him know that, though he was displeased with him, yet he had not deserted him. Some of the captains that knew him perceived their mistake, and so retired from the pursuit of him; but it is said (<reference osisRef="2Chr.18.31">2 Chron. xviii. 31</reference>) that <hi type="italic">God moved them</hi> (for he has all hearts in his hand) <hi type="italic">to depart from him.</hi> To him he cried out, not in cowardice, but devotion, and from him his relief came: Ahab was in no care to succour him. God is a friend that will not fail us when other friends do. <div eID="gen7045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7046" type="x-p"/> IV. Ahab receives his mortal wound in the battle, notwithstanding his endeavours to secure himself in the habit of a private sentinel. Let no man think to hide himself from God's judgment, no, not in masquerade. <hi type="italic">Thy hand shall find out all thy enemies,</hi> whatever disguise they are in, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.34">v. 34</reference>. The Syrian that shot him little thought of doing such a piece of service to God and his king; for he <hi type="italic">drew a bow at a venture,</hi> not aiming particularly at any man, yet God so directed the arrow that, 1. He hit the right person, the man that was marked for destruction, whom, if they had taken alive, as was designed, perhaps Ben-hadad would have spared. Those cannot escape with life whom God hath doomed to death. 2. He hit him in the right place, <hi type="italic">between the joints of the harness,</hi> the only place about him where this arrow of death could find entrance. No armour is of proof against the darts of divine vengeance. Case the criminal in steel, and it is all one, <hi type="italic">he that made him can make his sword to approach him.</hi> That which to us seems altogether casual is done by the determinate counsel and fore-knowledge of God. <div eID="gen7046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7047" type="x-p"/> V. The army is dispersed by the enemy and sent home by the king. Either Jehoshaphat or Ahab ordered the retreat of the sheep, when the shepherd was smitten: <hi type="italic">Every man to his city,</hi> for it is to no purpose to attempt any thing more, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.36">v. 36</reference>. Ahab himself lived long enough to see that part of Micaiah's prophecy accomplished that all Israel should be scattered <hi type="italic">upon the mountains of Gilead</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.17">v. 17</reference>), and perhaps with his dying lips did himself give orders for it; for though he would be carried out of the army, to have his wounds dressed (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.34">v. 34</reference>), yet he would be <hi type="italic">held up in his chariot,</hi> to see if his army were victorious. But, when he saw the battle increase against them, his spirits sunk, and he died, but his death was so lingering that he had time to feel himself die; and we may well imagine with what horror he now reflected upon the wickedness he had committed, the warnings he had slighted, Baal's altars, Naboth's vineyard, Micaiah's imprisonment. Now he sees himself flattered into his own ruin, and Zedekiah's horns of iron pushing, not the Syrians, but himself, into destruction. Thus is he <hi type="italic">brought to the king of terrors</hi> without <hi type="italic">hope in his death.</hi> <div eID="gen7047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7048" type="x-p"/> VI. The royal corpse is brought to Samaria and buried there (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.37">v. 37</reference>), and hither are brought the bloody chariot and bloody armour in which he died, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.38">v. 38</reference>. One particular circumstance is taken notice of, because there was in it the accomplishment of a prophecy, that when they brought the chariot to the pool of Samaria, to be washed, the dogs (and swine, says the LXX.) gathered about it, and, as is usual, <hi type="italic">licked the blood,</hi> or, as some think, the water in which it was washed, with which the blood was mingled: the dogs made no difference between royal blood and other blood. Now Naboth's blood was avenged (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.19">ch. xxi. 19</reference>), and that word of David, as well as Elijah's word, was fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.23">Ps. lxviii. 23</reference>), <hi type="italic">That thy foot may be dipped in the blood of thy enemies, and the tongue of thy dogs in the same.</hi> The dogs licking the guilty blood was perhaps designed to represent the terrors that prey upon the guilty soul after death. <div eID="gen7048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7049" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> The story of Ahab is here concluded in the usual form, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.39-1Kgs.22.40">v. 39, 40</reference>. Among his works mention is made of an ivory house which he built, so called because many parts of it were inlaid with ivory; perhaps it was intended to vie with the stately palace of the kings of Judah, which Solomon built.
entries.20532d9db2be734a7f21d1e833fba098a04070ea: <div eID="gen7049" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jehoshaphat's Death. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 897.)</title> <div sID="gen7050" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">41</hi> And Jehoshaphat the son of Asa began to reign over Judah in the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel. <hi type="super">42</hi> Jehoshaphat <hi type="italic">was</hi> thirty and five years old when he began to reign; and he reigned twenty and five years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Azubah the daughter of Shilhi. <hi type="super">43</hi> And he walked in all the ways of Asa his father; he turned not aside from it, doing <hi type="italic">that which was</hi> right in the eyes of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : nevertheless the high places were not taken away; <hi type="italic">for</hi> the people offered and burnt incense yet in the high places. <hi type="super">44</hi> And Jehoshaphat made peace with the king of Israel. <hi type="super">45</hi> Now the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, and his might that he showed, and how he warred, <hi type="italic">are</hi> they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah? <hi type="super">46</hi> And the remnant of the sodomites, which remained in the days of his father Asa, he took out of the land. <hi type="super">47</hi> <hi type="italic">There was</hi> then no king in Edom: a deputy <hi type="italic">was</hi> king. <hi type="super">48</hi> Jehoshaphat made ships of Tharshish to go to Ophir for gold: but they went not; for the ships were broken at Ezion-geber. <hi type="super">49</hi> Then said Ahaziah the son of Ahab unto Jehoshaphat, Let my servants go with thy servants in the ships. But Jehoshaphat would not. <hi type="super">50</hi> And Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers, and was buried with his fathers in the city of David his father: and Jehoram his son reigned in his stead. <hi type="super">51</hi> Ahaziah the son of Ahab began to reign over Israel in Samaria the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and reigned two years over Israel. <hi type="super">52</hi> And he did evil in the sight of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and walked in the way of his father, and in the way of his mother, and in the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin: <hi type="super">53</hi> For he served Baal, and worshipped him, and provoked to anger the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, according to all that his father had done. <div eID="gen7050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7051" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A short account of the reign of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, of which we shall have a much fuller narrative in the book of Chronicles, and of the greatness and goodness of that prince, neither of which was lessened or sullied by any thing but his intimacy with the house of Ahab, which, upon several accounts, was a diminution to him. His confederacy with Ahab in war we have already found dangerous to him, and his confederacy with Ahaziah his son in trade sped no better. He offered to go partner with him in a fleet of merchant-ships, that should fetch gold from Ophir, as Solomon's navy did, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.49">v. 49</reference>. See <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.35-2Chr.20.36">2 Chron. xx. 35, 36</reference>. But, while they were preparing to set sail, they were exceedingly damaged and disabled by a storm (<hi type="italic">broken at Ezion-geber</hi>), which a prophet gave Jehoshaphat to understand was a rebuke to him for his league with wicked Ahaziah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.37">2 Chron. xx. 37</reference>); and therefore, as we are told here (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.49">v. 49</reference>), when Ahaziah desired a second time to be a partner with him, or, if that could not be obtained, that he might but send his servants with some effects of board Jehoshaphat's ships, he refused: <hi type="italic">Jehoshaphat would not.</hi> The rod of God, expounded by the word of God, had effectually broken him off from his confederacy with that ungodly unhappy prince. Better buy wisdom dear than be without it; but experience is therefore said to be the mistress of fools because those are fools that will not learn till they are taught by experience, and particularly till they are taught the danger of associating with wicked people. Now Jehoshaphat's reign appears here to have been none of the longest, but one of the best. 1. It was none of the longest, for he reigned but twenty-five years (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.42">v. 42</reference>), but then it was in the prime of his time, between thirty-five and sixty, and these twenty-five, added to his father's happy forty-one, give us a grateful idea of the flourishing condition of the kingdom of Judah, and of religion in it, for a great while, even when things were very bad, upon all accounts, in the kingdom of Israel. If Jehoshaphat reigned not so long as his father, to balance this he had not those blemishes on the latter end of his reign that his father had (<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.9-2Chr.16.10">2 Chron. xvi. 9, 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.12">12</reference>), and it is better for a man that has been in reputation for wisdom and honour to die in the midst of it than to outlive it. 2. Yet is was one of the best, both in respect of piety and prosperity. (1.) He did well: He <hi type="italic">did that which was right in the eyes of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.43">v. 43</reference>), observed the commands of his God, and trod in the steps of his good father; and he persevered therein: He <hi type="italic">turned not aside from it.</hi> Yet every man's character has some <hi type="italic">but</hi> or other, so had his; the <hi type="italic">high places were not taken away,</hi> no not out of Judah and Benjamin, though those tribes lay so near Jerusalem that they might easily bring their offerings and incense to the altar there, and could not pretend, as some other of the tribes, the inconveniency of lying remote. But old corruptions are with difficulty rooted out, especially when they have formerly had the patronage of those that were good, as the high places had of Samuel, Solomon, and some others. (2.) His affairs did well. He prevented the mischiefs which had attended their wars with the kingdom of Israel, establishing a lasting peace (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.44">v. 44</reference>), which would have been a greater blessing if he had contented himself with a peace, and not carried it on to an affinity with Israel; he put a deputy, or viceroy, in Edom, so that the kingdom was tributary to him (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.47">v. 47</reference>), and therein the prophecy concerning Esau and Jacob was fulfilled, that <hi type="italic">the elder should serve the younger.</hi> And, in general, mention is made of his might and his wars, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.45">v. 45</reference>. He pleased God, and God blessed him with strength and success. His death is spoken of (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.50">v. 50</reference>), to shut up his story, yet, in the history of the kings of Israel, we find mention of him afterwards, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.7">2 Kings iii. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen7051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7052" type="x-p"/> II. The beginning of the story of Ahaziah the son of Ahab, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.51-1Kgs.22.53">v. 51-53</reference>. His reign was very short, not two years. Some sinners God makes quick work with. It is a very bad character that is here given him. He not only kept up Jeroboam's idolatry, but the worship of Baal likewise; though he had heard of the ruin of Jeroboam's family, and had seen his own father drawn into destruction by the prophets of Baal, who had often been proved false prophets, yet he received no instruction, took no warning, but followed the example of his wicked father and the counsel of his more wicked mother Jezebel, who was still living. Miserable are the children that not only derive a stock of corruption from their parents, but are thus taught by them to trade with it; and unhappy, most unhappy parents, are those that help to damn their children's souls.  <chapter eID="1Kgs.22"/> <div eID="gen7052" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen6497" osisID="1Kgs" type="book"/>

entries.21857a729dfee0642a331a71279147f6669e32ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3321"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 22</title> <div sID="gen4662" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.1-1Kgs.22.36">1Ki 22:1-36</reference>. Ahab Slain at Ramoth-gilead.<div eID="gen4662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4663" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3321"/><hi type="bold">1. continued three years without war between Syria and Israel--</hi>The disastrous defeat of Ben-hadad had so destroyed his army and exhausted the resources of his country, that, however eager, he was unable to recommence active hostilities against Israel. But that his hereditary enmity remained unsubdued, was manifest by his breach of faith concerning the treaty by which he had engaged to restore all the cities which his father had seized (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.34">1Ki 20:34</reference>). <div eID="gen4663" type="x-p"/>
entries.950a439b74759dacb56278099135af5179980771: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3322"/><div sID="gen4664" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3322"/><hi type="bold">2. Jehoshaphat the king of Judah came down to the king of Israel--</hi>It was singular that a friendly league between the sovereigns of Israel and Judah should, for the first time, have been formed by princes of such opposite characters--the one pious, the other wicked. Neither this league nor the matrimonial alliance by which the union of the royal families was more closely cemented, met the Lord's approval (<reference osisRef="2Chr.19.2">2Ch 19:2</reference>). It led, however, to a visit by Jehoshaphat, whose reception in Samaria was distinguished by the most lavish hospitality (<reference osisRef="2Chr.18.2">2Ch 18:2</reference>). The opportunity of this visit was taken advantage of, to push an object on which Ahab's heart was much set. <div eID="gen4664" type="x-p"/>
entries.19c43faab86e49d62877caae9cdb213cadedd54f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3323"/><div sID="gen4665" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3323"/><hi type="bold">3-8. Know ye that Ramoth in Gilead is ours--</hi>a Levitical and free town on the north border of Gad (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.43">De 4:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.21.38">Jos 21:38</reference>), on the site of the present Salt Lake, in the province of Belka. It lay within the territories of the Israelitish monarch, and was unjustly alienated; but whether it was one of the cities usurped by the first Ben-hadad, which his son had promised to restore, or was retained for some other reasons, the sacred historian has not mentioned. In the expedition which Ahab meditated for the recovery of this town, the aid of Jehoshaphat was asked and promised (see <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.3">2Ch 18:3</reference>). Previous to declaring hostilities, it was customary to consult the prophets (see on <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.8">1Sa 28:8</reference>); and Jehoshaphat having expressed a strong desire to know the Lord's will concerning this war, Ahab assembled four hundred of his prophets. These could not be either the prophets of Baal or of Ashteroth (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.19">1Ki 18:19</reference>), but seem (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.12">1Ki 22:12</reference>) to have been false prophets, who conformed to the symbolic calf-worship of Jehovah. Being the creatures of Ahab, they unanimously predicted a prosperous issue to the war. But dissatisfied with them, Jehoshaphat inquired if there was any true prophet of the Lord. Ahab agreed, with great reluctance, to allow Micaiah to be summoned. He was the only true prophet then to be found residing in Samaria, and he had to be brought out of prison (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.26">1Ki 22:26</reference>), into which, according to Josephus, he had been cast on account of his rebuke to Ahab for sparing the king of Syria. <div eID="gen4665" type="x-p"/>
entries.a3d6659be76ae01d16c15cda70a9fc3da922a41a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3324"/><div sID="gen4666" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3324"/><hi type="bold">10. a void place--</hi>literally, "a threshing-floor," formed at the gate of Samaria. <div eID="gen4666" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f655fc61c29bb431ae4f39f65cf2b4ec2db2b8c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3325"/><div sID="gen4667" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3325"/><hi type="bold">11. Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made him horns of iron--</hi>Small projections, of the size and form of our candle extinguishers (worn in many parts of the East as military ornaments), were worn by the Syrians of that time, and probably by the Israelite warriors also. Zedekiah, by assuming two horns, personated two heroes, and, pretending to be a prophet, wished in this manner to represent the kings of Israel and Judah in a military triumph. It was a symbolic action, to impart greater force to his language (see <reference osisRef="Deut.33.17">De 33:17</reference>); but it was little more than a flourish with a spontoon [Calmet, Fragments]. <div eID="gen4667" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a5dace906aa47746d47fb9dced344aebe458d12: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3326"/><div sID="gen4668" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3326"/><hi type="bold">14-17. what the Lord saith unto me, that will I speak--</hi>On the way the messenger who conducted [Micaiah] to the royal presence informed him of the tenor of the prophecies already given and recommended him to agree with the rest, no doubt from the kindly motive of seeing him released from imprisonment. But Micaiah, inflexibly faithful to his divine mission as a prophet, announced his purpose to proclaim honestly whatever God should bid him. On being asked by the king, "Shall I go against Ramoth-gilead, or shall I forbear?" the prophet gave precisely the same answer as the previous oracles that had been consulted; but it must have been given in a sarcastic tone and in ironical mockery of their way of speaking. Being solemnly urged to give a serious and truthful answer, Micaiah then declared the visionary scene the Spirit had revealed to him;-- <div eID="gen4668" type="x-p"/>
entries.27994562ed14005239356451de4cf31e04bf962f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3328"/><div sID="gen4670" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3328"/><hi type="bold">18-23. Did I not tell thee that he would prophesy no good concerning me, but evil?--</hi>Since Ahab was disposed to trace this unwelcome truth to personal enmity, Micaiah proceeded fearlessly to tell the incensed monarch in full detail what had been revealed to him. The Hebrew prophets, borrowing their symbolic pictures from earthly scenes, described God in heaven as a king in His kingdom. And as earthly princes do nothing of importance without asking the advice of their counsellors, God is represented as consulting about the fate of Ahab. This prophetic language must not be interpreted literally, and the command must be viewed as only a permission to the lying spirit (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.34">Ro 11:34</reference>) [Calmet]. <div eID="gen4670" type="x-p"/>
entries.91f2620563b72d7918b78801d07e56aea99e0b81: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3329"/><div sID="gen4671" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3329"/><hi type="bold">24-25. Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah went near, and smote Micaiah on the cheek--</hi>The insolence of this man, the leader of the false prophets, seems to have been provoked by jealousy at Micaiah's assumed monopoly of the spirit of inspiration. This mode of smiting, usually with a shoe, is both severe and ignominious. The calm reply of the Lord's prophet consisted in announcing the fate of the false prophets who suffered as the advisers of the disastrous expedition. <div eID="gen4671" type="x-p"/>
entries.915860f8cf04da27d5f57d73b87adafb78b2260a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3330"/><div sID="gen4672" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3330"/><hi type="bold">26-28. Take Micaiah, ... Put this fellow in prison--</hi>Ahab, under the impulse of vehement resentment, remands the prophet until his return. <div eID="gen4672" type="x-p"/>
entries.849b59259ded863f4c04dc989a4c2f692993bfbc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3332"/><div sID="gen4674" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3332"/><hi type="bold">29-38. went up to Ramoth-gilead--</hi>The king of Israel, bent on this expedition, marched, accompanied by his ally, with all his forces to the siege; but on approaching the scene of action, his courage failed, and, hoping to evade the force of Micaiah's prophecy by a secret stratagem, he assumed the uniform of a subaltern, while he advised Jehoshaphat to fight in his royal attire. The Syrian king, with a view either to put the speediest end to the war, or perhaps to wipe out the stain of his own humiliation (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.31">1Ki 20:31</reference>), had given special instructions to his generals to single out Ahab, and to take or kill him, as the author of the war. The officers at first directed their assault on Jehoshaphat, but, becoming aware of their mistake, desisted. Ahab was wounded by a random arrow, which, being probably poisoned, and the state of the weather increasing the virulence of the poison, he died at sunset. The corpse was conveyed to Samaria; and, as the chariot which brought it was being washed, in a pool near the city, from the blood that had profusely oozed from the wound, the dogs, in conformity with Elijah's prophecy, came and licked it [1Ki 21:19]. Ahab was succeeded by his son Ahaziah [1Ki 22:40]. <chapter eID="1Kgs.22"/><div eID="gen4674" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen4250" osisID="1Kgs" type="book"/>

entries.68e7282fb6a9d77ad47b739cb869197d1e8e1de8: <div eID="gen12331" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen12332" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12333" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12333" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12332" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12334" type="x-p"/> Jehoshaphat King of Judah, and Ahab King of Israel, unite against the Syrians, in order to recover Ramoth-gilead, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.1-1Kgs.22.4">1Kgs 22:1-4</reference>. They inquire of false prophets, who promise them success. Micaiah, a true prophet, foretells the disasters of the war, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.5-1Kgs.22.17">1Kgs 22:5-17</reference>. A lying spirit in the mouths of Ahab's prophets persuades Ahab to go up against Ramoth, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.18-1Kgs.22.29">1Kgs 22:18-29</reference>. The confederate armies are routed, and the king of Israel slain, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.30-1Kgs.22.36">1Kgs 22:30-36</reference>. Death and burial of Ahab, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.37-1Kgs.22.40">1Kgs 22:37-40</reference>. Character of Jehoshaphat, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.41-1Kgs.22.47">1Kgs 22:41-47</reference>. He makes a fleet in order to go to Ophir for gold, which is wrecked at Ezion-geber, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.48">1Kgs 22:48</reference>. His death, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.49">1Kgs 22:49</reference>. He is succeeded by his son Jehoram, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.50">1Kgs 22:50</reference>. Ahaziah succeeds his father Ahab, and reigns wickedly, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.51">1Kgs 22:51</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.52">1Kgs 22:52</reference>. <div eID="gen12334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12335" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen12335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12336" type="x-p"/> Three years without war - That is, from the time that Ahab made the covenant with Ben-hadad, mentioned <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.34">1Kgs 20:34</reference>. And probably in that treaty it was stipulated that Ramoth-gilead should be restored to Israel; which not being done, Ahab formed a confederacy with Judah, and determined to take it by force.
entries.b79b9dda193a5d52e86b2ceba71500307eb5baf4: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen12336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12337" type="x-p"/> Wilt thou go with me - We find that there was a good understanding between Jehoshaphat and Ahab, which no doubt was the consequence of a matrimonial alliance between the son of the former, Jehoram, and the daughter of the latter, Athaliah; see <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.1">2Chr 18:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.18">2Kgs 8:18</reference>. This coalition did not please God, and Jehoshaphat is severely reproved for it by Jehu the seer, <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.1-2Chr.19.3">2Chr 19:1-3</reference>.
entries.894b279bdb3d97ae98e02f97d9e696d6d5dc56da: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen12337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12338" type="x-p"/> About four hundred men - These were probably the prophets of Asherah or Venus, maintained by Jezebel, who were not present at the contention on Mount Carmel. See <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.19">1Kgs 18:19</reference>, etc.
entries.d0faf7fbfe045d86c3e3d5358bd8c8f2b98cc608: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen12338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12339" type="x-p"/> Micaiah the son of Imlah - The Jews suppose that it was this prophet who reproved Ahab for dismissing Ben-hadad, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.35">1Kgs 20:35</reference>, etc. And that it was because of the judgments with which he had threatened him, that Ahab hated him: I hate him, for he doth not prophesy good concerning me, but evil.
entries.aab522d29bddd94f23d8765bd6d00ee96fa78307: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen12339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12340" type="x-p"/> The king of Israel called an officer - סריס saris, literally a eunuch; probably a foreigner, for it was not lawful to disgrace an Israelite by reducing him to such a state.
entries.152276c3ef8b0a92b54594b1f63dc9812b061ae6: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen12340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12341" type="x-p"/> Zedekiah - made him horns of iron - This was in imitation of that sort of prophecy which instructed by significative actions. This was frequent among the prophets of the Lord.
entries.8d0b053d643f0e46e0d7954a841948b0ee586363: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen12341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12342" type="x-p"/> The words of the prophets declare good - What notion could these men have of prophecy, when they supposed it was in the power of the prophet to model the prediction as he pleased, and have the result accordingly?
entries.cb79f5a9e1b0c70fd9ccf72af552c2b78758752b: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen12342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12343" type="x-p"/> Go, and prosper - This was a strong irony; as if he had said, All your prophets have predicted success; you wish me to speak as they speak: Go, and prosper; for the Lord will deliver it into the hand of the king. These were the precise words of the false prophets, (see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.6">1Kgs 22:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.12">1Kgs 22:12</reference>), and were spoken by Micaiah in such a tone and manner as at once showed to Ahab that he did not believe them; hence the king adjures him, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.16">1Kgs 22:16</reference>, that he would speak to him nothing but truth; and on this the prophet immediately relates to him the prophetic vision which pointed out the disasters which ensued. <div eID="gen12343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12344" type="x-p"/> It is worthy of remark that this prophecy of the king's prophets is couched in the same ambiguous terms by which the false prophets in the heathen world endeavored to maintain their credit, while they deluded their votaries. The reader will observe that the word it is not in the original: The Lord will deliver It into the hand of the king; and the words are so artfully constructed that they may be interpreted for or against; so that, be the event whatever it might, the juggling prophet could save his credit by saying he meant what had happened. Thus then the prophecy might have been understood: The Lord will deliver (Ramoth-gilead) into the king's (Ahab's) hand; or, The Lord will deliver (Israel) into the king's hand; i.e., into the hand of the king of Syria. And Micaiah repeats these words of uncertainty in order to ridicule them and expose their fallacy. <div eID="gen12344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12345" type="x-p"/> The following oracles among the heathens were of this same dubious nature, in order that the priests' credit might be saved, let the event turn out as it might. Thus the Delphic oracle spoke to Croesus words which are capable of a double meaning, and which he understood to his own destruction: - <div eID="gen12345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12346" type="x-p"/> Croesus, Halym penetrans, magnam subvertet opum vim, <div eID="gen12346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12347" type="x-p"/> Which says, in effect: - "If you march against Cyrus, he will either overthrow you, or you will overthrow him." <div eID="gen12347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12348" type="x-p"/> He trusted in the latter, the former took place. He was deluded, and yet the oracle maintained its credit. So in the following: - <div eID="gen12348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12349" type="x-p"/> Aio te, Aeacida, Romanos vincere posse <div eID="gen12349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12350" type="x-p"/> Ibis redibis nunquam in bello peribis. <div eID="gen12350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12351" type="x-p"/> Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, understood by this that he should conquer the Romans, against whom he was then making war; but the oracle could be thus translated: "The Romans shall overcome thee." He trusted in the former, made unsuccessful war, and was overcome; and yet the juggling priest saved his credit. The latter line is capable of two opposite meanings: - "Thou shalt go, thou shalt return, thou shalt never perish in war." <div eID="gen12351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12352" type="x-p"/> Or, "Thou shalt go, thou shalt never return, thou shalt perish in war." <div eID="gen12352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12353" type="x-p"/> When prophecies and oracles were not delivered in this dubious way, they were generally couched in such intricate and dark terms that the assistance of the oracle was necessary to explain the oracle, and then it was ignotum per ignotius, a dark saying paraphrased by one yet more obscure.
entries.47ba5de379e3174e242d171eb3350ac237910297: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen12353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12354" type="x-p"/> These have no master - Here the prophet foretells the defeat of Israel, and the death of the king; they were as sheep that had not a shepherd, people that had no master, the political shepherd and master (Ahab) shall fall in battle.
entries.cbed5f7d142ef55c08cd0361f5a8b3d3b3b84a55: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen12354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12355" type="x-p"/> I saw the Lord sitting on his throne - This is a mere parable, and only tells in figurative language, what was in the womb of providence, the events which were shortly to take place, the agents employed in them, and the permission on the part of God for these agents to act. Micaiah did not choose to say before this angry and impious king, "Thy prophets are all liars; and the devil, the father of lies, dwells in them;" but he represents the whole by this parable, and says the same truths in language as forcible, but less offensive.
entries.5aced9b04b0855ec5fe05c7593496e7d3fc342cc: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen12355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12356" type="x-p"/> Go forth, and do so - This is no more than, "God has permitted the spirit of lying to influence the whole of thy prophets; and he now, by my mouth, apprises thee of this, that thou mayest not go and fall at Ramoth-gilead." Never was a man more circumstantially and fairly warned; he had counsels from the God of truth, and counsels from the spirit of falsity; he obstinately forsook the former and followed the latter. He was shown by this parable how every thing was going on, and that all was under the control and direction of God, and that still it was possible for him to make that God his friend whom by his continual transgressions he had made his enemy; but he would not: his blood was therefore upon his own head.
entries.e4ad39232e9310d38a5d6c939afd1200f4b41519: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen12356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12357" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath put a lying spirit - He hath permitted or suffered a lying spirit to influence thy prophets. Is it requisite again to remind the reader that the Scriptures repeatedly represent God as doing what, in the course of his providence, he only permits or suffers to be done? Nothing can be done in heaven, in earth, or hell, but either by his immediate energy or permission. This is the reason why the Scripture speaks as above.
entries.2870318dda808fb32e62541c16d19937c2934669: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen12357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12358" type="x-p"/> Which way went the Spirit of the Lord from me - This is an expression of as great insolence as the act was of brutal aggression. "Did the Spirit of the Lord, who rests solely upon me, condescend to inspire thee? Was it at this ear [where he smote him] that it entered, in order to hold communion with thee?" Josephus tells an idle rabbinical tale about this business, which is as unworthy of repetition as it is of credit. See his Antiq. of the Jews, book viii., c. 10.
entries.b253e9332fd35c4b1f2724358b3628391b1b656f: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen12358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12359" type="x-p"/> When thou shalt go into an inner chamber - It is probable that this refers to some Divine judgment which fell upon this deceiver. Hearing of the tragical result of the battle, he no doubt went into a secret place to hide himself from the resentment of Jezebel, and the Israelitish courtiers, and there it is probable he perished; but how, when, or where, is not mentioned.
entries.ca8e83f3b363a9e00678b3429f78d830e523faea: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen12359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12360" type="x-p"/> Feed him with bread of affliction - Deprive him of all the conveniences and comforts of life; treat him severely; just keep him alive, that he may see my triumph.
entries.9c926bd67ed1ba58d03c89d7c5ea517c8840fd3f: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen12360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12361" type="x-p"/> I will disguise myself - Probably he had heard of the orders given by Ben-hadad to his thirty-two captains, to fight with the king of Israel only; that is, to make their most powerful attack where he commanded, in order to take him prisoner, that he might lead him captive whose captive he formerly was; and therefore he disguised himself that he might not be known. <div eID="gen12361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12362" type="x-p"/> But put thou on thy robes - What is meant by this? He could not mean, "Appear as the king of Judah, for they will not molest thee, as the matter of contention lies between them and me;" this is Jarchi's turn. For if Jehoshaphat aided Ahab, is it to be supposed that the Syrians would spare him in battle? A general in the civil wars of England, when he had brought his army in sight of their foes, thus addressed them: "Yonder are your enemies; if you do not kill them, they will kill you." So it might be said in the case of Jehoshaphat and the Syrians. <div eID="gen12362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12363" type="x-p"/> The Septuagint gives the clause a different and more intelligible turn: "I will cover (conceal) myself, and enter into the battle; και συ ενδυσαι τον ἱματισμον μου, but put thou on My robes." And does it not appear that he did put on Ahab's robes? And was it not this that caused the Syrians to mistake him for the king of Israel? <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.32">1Kgs 22:32</reference>.
entries.48325b6fefbe1de48725ec2d5410292474f8203b: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen12363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12364" type="x-p"/> Drew a bow at a venture - It is supposed that he shot, as the archers in general did, not aiming at any person in particular. <div eID="gen12364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12365" type="x-p"/> The word לתמו lethummo, which we translate in his simplicity, has been variously understood; in his integrity, his uprightness; in his perfection; i.e., to the utmost of his skill and strength. This is most probably the meaning; and may imply both aim and power, having his butt full in view. <div eID="gen12365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12366" type="x-p"/> In cases where the archers wished to do the greatest execution, they bent their bows, and pulled till the subtending string drew back the arrow up to its head. This they could not do always, because it required their whole strength; and they could not put forth their utmost effort each time and continue to discharge many shots.
