Our old national ballad of the Chevy-chace mentions the slaying of Sir Hugh Montgomery, who had slain Earl Percy, in nearly the same way that Ahab appears to have been shot: - "And thus did both these nobles die, <div eID="gen12366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12367" type="x-p"/> Whose courage none could stain: <div eID="gen12367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12368" type="x-p"/> An English archer then perceived <div eID="gen12368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12369" type="x-p"/> His noble lord was slain, <div eID="gen12369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12370" type="x-p"/> Who had a bow bent in his hand <div eID="gen12370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12371" type="x-p"/> Made of a trusty tree; <div eID="gen12371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12372" type="x-p"/> An arrow, of a cloth-yard long, <div eID="gen12372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12373" type="x-p"/> Up to the head drew he; Against <div eID="gen12373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12374" type="x-p"/> Sir Hugh Montgomery then <div eID="gen12374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12375" type="x-p"/> So right his shaft he set, <div eID="gen12375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12376" type="x-p"/> The gray goose wing that was thereon <div eID="gen12376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12377" type="x-p"/> In his heart's blood was wet." <div eID="gen12377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12378" type="x-p"/> Between the joints of the harness - "Between the cuirass and the lower part of the helmet;" and then the arrow must pass through the neck, just above the breast: or "between the cuirass and the cuissarts;" and then the arrow must pass through the abdomen, or just where the armor of the thighs joins to that which covers the breast and belly. <div eID="gen12378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12379" type="x-p"/> The Vulgate has Inter pulmonem et stomachum; "Between the lungs and the stomach;" consequently, in the region of the heart.
entries.10b1019f122a58c13d0e3e7ebb88122c1a2d4a71: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen12379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12380" type="x-p"/> The king was stayed up - He did not wish his misfortune should be known, lest his troops should be discouraged.
entries.470c1f8faa1c0ee093325b5fad5fdb7b02d0fae4: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen12380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12381" type="x-p"/> Every man to his city - It appears that the Israelites and Jews maintained the fight the whole of the day; but when at evening the king died, and this was known, there was a proclamation made, probably with the consent of both Syrians and Israelites, that the war was over. Ahab being dead, his subjects did not choose to contend for Ramoth-gilead; so the Israelites went to their own cities, and the Syrians to their own country.
entries.75b970d2e03031a12634783154c1745b5a5a7025: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen12381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12382" type="x-p"/> The dogs licked up his blood - Some of the rabbins think that this was in the very place where Naboth was stoned; see on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.19">1Kgs 21:19</reference> (note). The Septuagint translates this verse strangely: "And the swine and the dogs licked his blood, and the whores bathed themselves in his blood, according to the word of the Lord." It is certain that the Hebrew words, הזנות רחצו hazzonoth rachatsu, "washed his armor," might be translated as the Septuagint have done; "and the whores (or public women) washed," etc. And so the rabbins seem to have understood the words; but then they suppose that Jezebel had made him two images of prostitutes, which he had with him in the chariot. It is not worth inquiring into the use for which they say these images were made. See Kimchi and Jarchi.
entries.e3cd19e1cda5e0679f34b79e17cb9e6af3fc269f: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen12382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12383" type="x-p"/> Ivory house - A royal palace which he built in Samaria, decorated with ivory, and hence called the ivory house. Amos the prophet speaks against this luxury, <reference osisRef="Amo.3.15">Amo 3:15</reference>.
entries.46adf6a73de39287b73ee6a311177dc8620caab3: <hi type="bold">Verse 43</hi> <div eID="gen12383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12384" type="x-p"/> The high places were not taken away - In <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.6">2Chr 17:6</reference>, it is expressly said, that he did take away the high places. Allowing that the text is right in 2 Chron., the two places may be easily reconciled. There were two kinds of high places in the land: <div eID="gen12384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12385" type="x-p"/> 1. Those used for idolatrous purposes. <div eID="gen12385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12386" type="x-p"/> 2. Those that were consecrated to God, and were used before the temple was built. The former he did take away; the latter he did not. <div eID="gen12386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12387" type="x-p"/> But some think the parallel place in <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.6">2Chr 17:6</reference> is corrupted, and that, instead of ועוד הסיר veod hesir, "and moreover he took away," we should read, ולא הסיר velo hesir, "and he did Not take away."
entries.f80ff5e144e4e58d7356d9904ecff828e58e65db: <hi type="bold">Verse 46</hi> <div eID="gen12387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12388" type="x-p"/> The remnant of the sodomites - הקדש of the consecrated persons; or it may rather apply here to the system of pollution, effeminacy, and debauch. He destroyed the thing itself; the abominations of Priapus, and the rites of Venus, Baal, and Ashtaroth. No more of that impure worship was to be found in Judea.
entries.9711a183aca46ee6a575d7e7fac8eb23b25d41c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 47</hi> <div eID="gen12388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12389" type="x-p"/> There was no king in Edom - It is plain that the compiler of this book lived after the days of Jehoshaphat, in whose time the Edomites revolted; see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.22">2Kgs 8:22</reference>. David had conquered the Edomites, and they continued to be governed by deputies, appointed by the kings of Judah, till they recovered their liberty, as above. This note is introduced by the writer to account for Jehoshaphat's building ships at Ezion-geber, which was in the territory of the Edomites, and which showed them to be at that time under the Jewish yoke.
entries.beb3a4a510461e98ebfdb9932f9da86384fa405a: <hi type="bold">Verse 48</hi> <div eID="gen12389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12390" type="x-p"/> Ships of Tharshish to go to Ophir for gold - In the parallel place (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.36">2Chr 20:36</reference>) it is said that Jehoshaphat joined himself to Ahaziah, to make ships to go to Tharshish; and they made the ships in Ezion-geber. Concerning these places, and the voyage thither, see the notes on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.26-1Kgs.9.28">1Kgs 9:26-28</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.11">1Kgs 10:11</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.22">1Kgs 10:22</reference> (note). Some translate, instead of ships of Tharshish, ships of burden. See Houbigant, who expresses himself doubtful as to the meaning of the word.
entries.762e93c0b30a691b8d56bd1e76fac1579f89de78: <hi type="bold">Verse 49</hi> <div eID="gen12390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12391" type="x-p"/> But Jehoshaphat would not - It appears from the above cited place in Chronicles that Jehoshaphat did join in making and sending ships to Tharshish, and it is possible that what is here said is spoken of a second expedition, in which Jehoshaphat would not join Ahaziah. But instead of ולא אבה velo abah, "he would not," perhaps we should read ולו אבה velo abah, "he consented to him;" two words pronounced exactly in the same way, and differing but in one letter, viz., an א aleph for a ו vau. This reading, however, is not supported by any MS. or version; but the emendation seems just; for there are several places in these historical books in which there are mistakes of transcribers which nothing but violent criticism can restore, and to this it is dangerous to resort, but in cases of the last necessity. Critics have recommended the 48th and 49th verses to be read thus: "Jehoshaphat had built ships of burden at Ezion-geber, to go to Ophir for gold. 49. And Ahaziah, the son of Ahab, had said to Jehoshaphat, Let my servants, I pray thee, go with thy servants in the ships: to which Jehoshaphat consented. But the ships went not thither; for the ships were broken at Ezion-geber." This is Houbigant's translation, who contends that "the words of the 48th verse, but they went not, should be placed at the end of the 49th verse, for who can believe that the sacred writer should first relate that the ships were broken, and then that Ahaziah requested of Jehoshaphat that his servants might embark with the servants of Jehoshaphat?" This bold critic, who understood the Hebrew language better than any man in Europe, has, by happy conjectures, since verified by the testimony of MSS., removed the blots of many careless transcribers from the sacred volume.  <chapter eID="1Kgs.22"/> <div eID="gen12391" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen11420" osisID="1Kgs" type="book"/>

entries.4fd73df45596325d5018aae8fda3c4773a17765f: 1Ki 22:1 <div eID="gen5093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5094" type="x-p"/> Allied Campaign of Ahab and Jehoshaphat against the Syrians at Ramoth, and Death of Ahab (compare 2 Chron 18:2-34). - 1Ki 22:1. “And they rested three years; there was no war between Aram and Israel,” ישׁב here is to keep quiet, to undertake nothing, as in Jdg 5:17, etc. The subject to ויּשׁבוּ is Aram and Israel mentioned in the second clause. The length of time given here points back to the end of the war described in 1 Kings 20.
entries.cfa0d1c3480aa90be6a27fcdbc62e26e1d256071: 1Ki 22:2-4 <div eID="gen5094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5095" type="x-p"/> In the third year (not necessarily “towards the end of it,” as Thenius supposes, for Jehoshaphat’s visit preceded the renewal of the war) Jehoshaphat visited the king of Israel, with whom he had already formed a marriage alliance by marrying his son to Ahab’s daughter (<reference osisRef="2Chr.18.1">2Ch 18:1</reference>; 2Ki 8:18). Ahab then said to his servants that the king of Syria had kept the city of <hi type="italic">Ramoth</hi> in Gilead (probably situated on the site of the present <hi type="italic">Szalt</hi>: see at <reference osisRef="Deut.4.43">Deu 4:43</reference>), which he ought to have given up, according to the conditions of the peace in 1Ki 20:34, and asked Jehoshaphat whether he would go with him to the war against Ramoth, which the latter promised to do. “I as thou, my people as thy people, my horses as thy horses;” i.e., I am at thy service with the whole of my military power. In the place of the last words we have therefore in the Chronicles ועמך בּמּלחמה, “I am with thee in the war,” i.e., I will assist thee in the war.
entries.f7aaa37ea6929f5bcd7b4a63d85126c17dd6ada8: 1Ki 22:5-7 <div eID="gen5095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5096" type="x-p"/> But as Jehoshaphat wished also to inquire the word of the Lord concerning the war, Ahab gathered together about 400 prophets, who all predicted as out of one mouth a prosperous result to the campaign. These 400 prophets are neither the 400 prophets of Asherah who had not appeared upon Carmel when Elijah was there (1Ki 18:19-20), nor prophets of Baal, as some of the earlier commentators supposed, since Ahab could not inquire of them את־דּבר יהוה. On the other hand, they were not “true prophets of Jehovah and disciples of the prophets” (Cler., Then.), but prophets of Jehovah worshipped under the image of an ox, who practised prophesying as a trade without any call from God, and even if they were not in the pay of the idolatrous kings of Israel, were at any rate in their service. For Jehoshaphat did not recognise them as genuine prophets of Jehovah, but inquired whether there was not such a prophet still in existence (1Ki 22:7), that they might inquire the will of the Lord of him (מאותו).
entries.d3ad7195c86044d7f8388d12f4ca7abedbf723cb: 1Ki 22:8 <div eID="gen5096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5097" type="x-p"/> Ahab then named to him one, but one whom he hated, because he never prophesied good concerning him, but only evil,<note placement="foot">Just as Agamemnon says to Calchas in <hi type="italic">Il</hi>. iv. 106: μάντι κακῶν, ου ̓ πώποτέ μοι τὸ κρήγουν εἶπας, κ.τ.λ.</note> namely, <hi type="italic">Micah</hi> the son of Jimlah. Josephus and the Rabbins suppose him to have been the prophet, whose name is not given, who had condemned Ahab in the previous war for setting Benhadad at liberty (1Ki 20:35.). But there is no foundation for this, and it is mere conjecture. At any rate, Ahab had already come to know Micah as a prophet of evil, and, as is evident from 1Ki 22:26, had had him imprisoned on account of an unwelcome prophecy. Ahab’s dislike to this prophet had its root in the belief, which was connected with heathen notions of prophecy and conjuring, that the prophets stood in such a relation to the Deity that the latter necessarily fulfilled their will; a belief which had arisen from the fact that the predictions of true prophets always came to pass (see at Num 22:6 and Num 22:17).
entries.c978213526767b9aabbfd9a76e88905b440700e6: 1Ki 22:9 <div eID="gen5097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5098" type="x-p"/> By Jehoshaphat’s desire, Ahab nevertheless sent a chamberlain (סריס; see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.8.15">1Sa 8:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.37.36">Gen 37:36</reference>) to fetch Micah (מהרה, bring quickly).
entries.1215285b1392d53332b44c38df1b431b967e7467: 1Ki 22:10-12 <div eID="gen5098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5099" type="x-p"/> In the meantime the prophets of the calves continued to prophesy success before the two kings, who sat upon thrones “clothed in robes,” i.e., in royal attire, upon a floor in front of the gate of Samaria. גּרן, a threshing-floor, i.e., a levelled place in the open air. In order to give greater effect to their announcement, one of them, named <hi type="italic">Zedekiyah</hi> the son of Cnaanah, made himself iron horns, probably iron spikes held upon the head (Thenius), and said, “With these wilt thou thrust down Aram even to destruction.” This symbolical action was an embodiment of the figure used by Moses in the blessing of Joseph (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.17">Deu 33:17</reference>): “Buffalo horns are his (Joseph’s) horns, with them he thrusts down nations” (vid., Hengstenberg, <hi type="italic">Beitrr</hi>. ii. p. 131), and was intended to transfer to Ahab in the case before them that splendid promise which applied to the tribe of Ephraim. But the pseudo-prophet overlooked the fact that the fulfilment of the whole of the blessing of Moses was dependent upon fidelity to the Lord. All the rest of the prophets adopted the same tone, saying, “Go to Ramoth, and prosper,” i.e., and thou wilt prosper. (On this use of two imperatives see Ges. §130, 2).
entries.f7088d3759f220587981084104f4ef035ec33402: 1Ki 22:13-14 <div eID="gen5099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5100" type="x-p"/> The messenger who fetched Micah tried on the way to persuade him to prophesy success to the king as the other prophets had done; but Micah replied with a solemn oath, that he would only speak what Jehovah said to him.
entries.c4601e40d79a98d51e1031c39addf4edac936f40: 1Ki 22:15-17 <hi type="italic">Micah’s prophecy concerning the war, and his testimony against the lying prophets</hi>. - 1Ki 22:15, 1Ki 22:16. When Micah had come into the presence of the king, he replied to his question, “Shall we go against Ramoth?” etc., in just the same words as the pseudo-prophets, to show the king how he would speak if he were merely guided by personal considerations, as the others were. From the verbal agreement in his reply, and probably also from the tone in which he spoke, Ahab perceived that his words were ironical, and adjured him to speak only truth in the name of Jehovah. Micah then told him what he had seen in the spirit (1Ki 22:17): “I saw all Israel scatter itself upon the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd;” and then added the word of the Lord: “These have no master; let them return every one to his house in peace.” That is to say, Ahab would fall in the war against Ramoth in Gilead, and his army scatter itself without a leader upon the mountains of Gilead, and then every one would return home, without being pursued and slain by the enemy. Whilst Zedekiyah attempted to give greater emphasis to his prophecy by symbolically transferring to Ahab’s enterprise the success predicted by Moses, Micah, on the other hand, showed to the king out of the law that would really take place in the intended war, namely, that very state of things which Moses before his departure sought to avert from Israel, by the prayer that the Lord would set a man over the congregation to lead them out and in, that the congregation might not become as sheep that have no shepherd (Num 27:16-17).
entries.acb3c6a516da7a1cad5c2a2f0a7391b4482850c6: 1Ki 22:18 <div eID="gen5100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5101" type="x-p"/> But although Ahab had asked for a true word of the Lord, yet he endeavoured to attribute the unfavourable prophecy to Micah’s persona enmity, saying to Jehoshaphat, “Did I not tell thee that he prophesies nothing good concerning me, but only evil (misfortune)?”
entries.909010424aef5b266a23e4100f1c3ceefde1b85e: 1Ki 22:19-25 <div eID="gen5101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5102" type="x-p"/> Micah was not led astray, however, by this, but disclosed to him by a further revelation the hidden ground of the false prophecy of his 400 prophets. וגו שׁמע לכן, “therefore, sc. because thou thinkest so, hear the word of Jehovah: I saw the Lord sit upon His throne, and all the army of heaven stand around him (עליו עמד as in <reference osisRef="Gen.18.8">Gen 18:8</reference>, etc.) on His right hand and on His left. And the Lord said, Who will persuade Ahab to go up and fall at Ramoth in Gilead? and one spake so, the other so; and the spirit came forth (from the ranks of the rest), stood before Jehovah, and said, I will persuade him...I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets. And He (Jehovah) said, Persuade, and thou wilt also be able; go forth and do so. And now Jehovah has put a lying spirit into the mouth of all his prophets; but Jehovah (Himself) has spoken evil (through me) concerning thee.” The vision described by Micah was not merely a subjective drapery introduced by the prophet, but a simple communication of the real inward vision by which the fact had been revealed to him, that the prophecy of those 400 prophets was inspired by a lying spirit. The spirit (הרוּח) which inspired these prophets as a lying spirit is neither Satan, nor any evil spirit whatever, but, as the definite article and the whole of the context show, the personified spirit of prophecy, which is only so far a πνεῦμα ἀκάθαρτον τῆς πλάνης (Zec 13:2; 1Jo 4:6) and under the influence of Satan as it works as שׁקר רוּח in accordance with the will of God. For even the predictions of the false prophets, as we may see from the passage before us, and also from Zec 13:2 and the scriptural teaching in other passages concerning the spiritual principle of evil, were not mere inventions of human reason and fancy; but the false prophets as well as the true were governed by a supernatural spiritual principle, and, according to divine appointment, were under the influence of the evil spirit in the service of falsehood, just as the true prophets were moved by the Holy Spirit in the service of the Lord. The manner in which the supernatural influence of the lying spirit upon the false prophets is brought out in Micah’s vision is, that the spirit of prophecy (רוח הנבואה) offers itself to deceive Ahab as שׁקר רוּח in the false prophets. Jehovah sends this spirit, inasmuch as the deception of Ahab has been inflicted upon him as a judgment of God for his unbelief. But there is no statement here to the effect that this lying spirit proceeded from Satan, because the object of the prophet was simply to bring out the working of God in the deception practised upon Ahab by his prophets. - The words of Jehovah, “Persuade Ahab, thou wilt be able,” and “Jehovah has put a lying spirit,” etc., are not to be understood as merely expressing the permission of God, as the fathers and the earlier theologians suppose. According to the Scriptures, God does work evil, but without therefore willing it and bringing forth sin. The prophet’s view is founded upon this thought: Jehovah has ordained that Ahab, being led astray by a prediction of his prophets inspired by the spirit of lies, shall enter upon the war, that he may find therein the punishment of his ungodliness. As he would not listen to the word of the Lord in the mouth of His true servants, God had given him up (παρέδωκεν, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.24">Rom 1:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.26">Rom 1:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.28">Rom 1:28</reference>) in his unbelief to the working of the spirits of lying. But that this did not destroy the freedom of the human will is evident from the expression תּפתּה, “thou canst <hi type="italic">persuade</hi> him,” and still more clearly from תּוּכל גּם, “thou wilt also be able,” since they both presuppose the possibility of resistance to temptation on the part of man. <div eID="gen5102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5103" type="x-p"/> Zedekiah was so enraged at this unveiling of the spirit of lying by which the pseudo-prophets were impelled, that he smote Micah upon the cheek, and said (1Ki 22:24): “Where did the Spirit of Jehovah depart from me, to speak to thee?” To אי־זה the Chronicles add as an explanation, הדּרך: “by what way had he gone from me?” (cf. 2Ki 3:8, and Ewald, §326, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.) Zedekiah was conscious that he had not invented his prophecy himself, and therefore it was that he rose up with such audacity against Micah; but he only proved that it was not the Spirit of God which inspired him. If he had been inspired by the Spirit of the Lord, he would not have thought it necessary to try and give effect to his words by rude force, but he would have left the defence of his cause quietly to the Lord, as Micah did, who calmly replied to the zealot thus (1Ki 22:25): “Thou wilt see it (that the Spirit of Jehovah had departed from thee) on the day when thou shalt go from chamber to chamber to hide thyself” (החבה for החבא, see Ges. §75, Anm. 21). This was probably fulfilled at the close of the war, when Jezebel or the friends of Ahab made the pseudo-prophets suffer for the calamitous result; although there is nothing said about this in our history, which confines itself to the main facts.
entries.cd1873ec107f323fae310e1a2da36b399fd719f9: 1Ki 22:26-27 <div eID="gen5103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5104" type="x-p"/> But Ahab had Micah taken back to Amon the commander of the city, and to Joash the king’s son, with the command to put him in prison and to feed him with bread and water of affliction, till he came safe back (בּשׁלום) from the war. From the expression השׁיבהוּ, “lead him back,” it evidently follows that Micah had been fetched from the commander of the city, who had no doubt kept him in custody, as the city-prison was probably in his house. The opposite cannot be inferred from the words “put him into the prison;” for this command, when taken in connection with what follows, simply enjoins a more severe imprisonment.
entries.06473199c2cd93cd34d7b68d7f9f122b499c95c0: 1Ki 22:28 <div eID="gen5104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5105" type="x-p"/> In his consciousness of the divine truth of his announcement, Micah left the king with these words: “If thou come back safe, Jehovah has not spoken by me. Hear it, all ye nations.” עמּים does not mean people, for it is only in the antique language of the Pentateuch that the word has this meaning, but nations; and Micah thereby invokes not only the persons present as witnesses of the truth of his words, but the nations generally, Israel and the surrounding nations, who were to discern the truth of his word from the events which would follow (see at Mic 1:2).
entries.e620b28b7fda8b26374b0800060ff4c367b44668: 1Ki 22:29-40 <hi type="italic">The issue of the war, and death of Ahab</hi>. - 1Ki 22:29. Ahab, disregarding Micah’s prophecy, went on with the expedition, and was even joined by Jehoshaphat, of whom we should have thought that, after what had occurred, he at any rate would have drawn back. He was probably deterred by false shame, however, from retracting the unconditional promise of help which he had given to Ahab, merely in consequence of a prophetic utterance, which Ahab had brought against his own person from Micah’s subjective dislike. But Jehoshaphat narrowly escaped paying the penalty for it with his life (v. 32), and on his fortunate return to Jerusalem had to listen to a severe reproof from the prophet Jehu in consequence (<reference osisRef="2Chr.19.2">2Ch 19:2</reference>).
entries.8bbecc2e1fe66beee896f7207a7cd3fa90a5f4d5: 1Ki 22:41-42 1Ki 22:41-44, which give the age of Jehoshaphat when he ascended the throne, and the duration and character of his reign, are also found with slight deviations in <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.31-2Chr.20.33">2Ch 20:31-33</reference>, in the closing summary of the history of his reign.
entries.be7cb14803a7a17d046a4ab0815cd2053dca7c11: 1Ki 22:43 “He walked entirely in the way of his father Asa and departed not from it, to do what was well-pleasing to the Lord,” whereas Asa’s heart had become more estranged from the Lord in the last years of his reign (see 1Ki 15:18.). - On the worship of the high places (1Ki 22:43), see at 1Ki 15:14.
entries.a5cb16dd8686d1c97c67e61b813b9c46ac4f3d34: 1Ki 22:44 <div eID="gen5112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5113" type="x-p"/> He maintained peace with the king of Israel, i.e., with every one of the Israelitish kings who were contemporaneous with him, viz., Ahab, Ahaziah, and Joram, whereas hitherto the two kingdoms had assumed an attitude of hostility towards each other. Even if this friendly bearing towards Israel was laudable in itself, Jehoshaphat went beyond the bounds of what was allowable, since he formed a marriage alliance with the house of Ahab, by letting his son Joram marry a daughter of Ahab and Jezebel (<reference osisRef="2Chr.18.1">2Ch 18:1</reference>).
entries.f7c73f6302b322144ad0b86e0742fda8b5fc11cb: 1Ki 22:45-46 <div eID="gen5113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5114" type="x-p"/> The brave deeds (הגּבוּרה) which he performed include both his efforts to strengthen his kingdom, partly by raising fortifications and organizing the military force, and partly by instructing the people in the law and improving the administration of justice (<reference osisRef="2Chr.17.7-2Chr.17.19">2Ch 17:7-19</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.4-2Chr.19.11">2Ch 19:4-11</reference>), and also the wars which he waged, viz., the expeditions already mentioned. - For 1Ki 22:46 see 1Ki 15:12.
entries.518b31eaf7711f1e229777205d9f0ba005927909: 1Ki 22:47 “There was (then) no (real) king in Edom; a vicegerent was king,” i.e., governed the country. This remark is introduced here merely on account of what follows, namely, to show how it was that Jehoshaphat was able to attempt to restore the maritime trade with Ophir. If we observe this connection between the verse before us and what follows, we cannot infer from it, as Ewald does (<hi type="italic">Gesch</hi>. iii. pp. 464 and 474ff.), that the Edomites with Egyptian help had forced from Rehoboam both their liberty and also their right to have a king of their own blood, and had remained in this situation till Jehoshaphat completely subjugated them again. (See the remarks on 1Ki 11:21-22.) All that can be gathered from 2 Chron 20 is, that the Edomites, in league with the Ammonites and other desert tribes, made an incursion into Judah, and therefore tried to throw off the supremacy of Judah, but did not succeed in their attempt.
entries.2bffec110bf485a5b73d72142ed95cf45b90752d: 1Ki 22:48-50 <div eID="gen5114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5115" type="x-p"/> The brief notice concerning Jehoshaphat’s attempt to build Tarshish ships (for the word, see pp. 105f) for the voyage to Ophir is expanded in <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.36-2Chr.20.37">2Ch 20:36-37</reference>, where we learn that Jehoshaphat had allied himself with Ahaziah of Israel for this purpose, and that the prophet Eliezer predicted the destruction of his ships on account of this alliance. When the ships had been broken in pieces in Eziongeber, no doubt by a storm, Ahaziah made this fresh proposal to him: “Let my people sail with thy people;” but Jehoshaphat would not. Ahaziah evidently wanted to persuade Jehoshaphat to make another attempt, after the destruction of the ships which were first built; but Jehoshaphat did not agree to it any more, because it was impossible for him, after the fulfilment of Eliezer’s prediction, to expect a more favourable result. Thus the two accounts can be harmonized in a very simple manner, with the exception of the words “to go to Tarshish,” which we find in the Chronicles in the place of “to go to Ophir,” the reading in our text, and which sprang from an erroneous interpretation of the expression “ships of Tarshish” (see above, pp. 105f). The <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> עשׂר is an error of the pen for עשׂה (<hi type="italic">Keri</hi>); but נשׁבּרה (<hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi>) is not to be altered into נשׁבּרוּ, since the construction of a singular verb with the subject following in the plural is by no means rare (vid., Ewald, §317, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.). On Eziongeber and Ophir, see at 1Ki 9:26 and 1Ki 9:28.
entries.5a1b9968e54d6277f68bdfe84e4469e2608c3dea: 1Ki 22:51 <div eID="gen5115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5116" type="x-p"/> Reign of Ahaziah of Israel. - 1Ki 22:51. For the <hi type="italic">datum</hi> “in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat,” see at 2Ki 1:17.
entries.454060d106b8b25b4756d96c8d29f517e8e69a7d: 1Ki 22:52-53 <div eID="gen5116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5117" type="x-p"/> Ahaziah walked in the way of his father and his mother, who had introduced the worship of Baal into the kingdom, and in the way of Jeroboam, who had set up the calves (cf. 1Ki 16:30-33). - In 1Ki 22:53 it is again expressly added, that he adored and worshipped Baal, as in 1Ki 16:31. - With this general description of his character not only is the chapter brought to a close, but the first book of Kings also, - very unsuitably, however, since the further account of Ahaziah’s reign and of his death is given in 2 Kings 1 of the following book. It would have been incomparably more suitable to commence a fresh chapter with 1Ki 22:52, and indeed to commence the second book there also.  <chapter eID="1Kgs.22"/> <div eID="gen5117" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen4696" osisID="1Kgs" type="book"/>

                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In what manner went it? Forasmuch as I and my Brethren have consulted the Lord, and answered in his Name, and have the same spirit which thon pretendest to have, and not a lying spirit, as thou dost falsly and mali<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ciously affirm, How is it possible that the same spirit should tell us one thing, and thee the quite contrary?</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:299" />25 And Micaiah said, Behold, thou shalt see in that day, when thou shalt go <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> from chamber to chamber.</ns0:note> into <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> a cham<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ber in a chamber.</ns0:note> an inner cham<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ber to hide thy self <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Out of a just fear and expectation of the deserved punishment of a false Prophet, and of the great Author and Abettor of this pernicious War, and of <ns0:hi>Ahab</ns0:hi>'s de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />struction.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 And the king of Israel said, Take Micaiah, and carry him back <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">To wit, into Prison; where it seems, he was before shut up; for so the Lords Prophets were used by <ns0:hi>Ahab.</ns0:hi> And some think he was the deliverer of that unwelcome message, <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>hap.</ns0:hi> 20. 41, 42.</ns0:note> unto Amon the governour of the city, and to Joash the kings son:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 And say, Thus saith the king, Put this <ns0:hi>fel<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />low</ns0:hi> in the prison, and feed him with bread of af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fliction, and with water of affliction <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> With a very course and sparing Diet, whereby he may be onely supported to endure his torment. See <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 16. 3. 2 <ns0:hi>Chr.</ns0:hi> 18. 26. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 30. 20.</ns0:note>, until I come in peace <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Until I return in triumph, which I doubt not I shall do in spight of all his malici<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous suggestions to the contrary, and then I shall call him to an account for all his lyes and impudence.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 And Micaiah said, If thou return at all in peace, the LORD hath not spoken by me <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">I acknowledge my self to be an Impostor, and to de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />serve Death.</ns0:note>. And he said <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e. Micaiah,</ns0:hi> the person last named, being assured of the truth of his Prophecy, calls all the people to be witnesses of it.</ns0:note>, Hearken, O people, every one of you.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 So the king of Israel, and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Who, though a good man, yet was easily deceived in this matter; partly, because <ns0:hi>Micaiah</ns0:hi> was a person unknown to him, and both he and the other Prophets pretending to give their answer in the Name of the Lord, it seemed hard to him to determine the controversy, which onely the event could decide; and therefore it is no wonder if he was over<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />born by the vast disproportion of 400 Prophets to one, and by his Relation, and Obligation, and Affection to <ns0:hi>Ahab:</ns0:hi> and partly, because the War was Just and Lawful to recover his own rights, which the <ns0:hi>Syrian</ns0:hi> King unjustly detained from him.</ns0:note> went up to Ramoth-gilead.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30 And the king of Israel said unto Jehosha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phat, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> when he was to dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />guise himself, and enter into the battel.</ns0:note> I will disguise my self <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Put off my Imperial habit, that the <ns0:hi>Syrians</ns0:hi> may not know me, and direct their main Force against me; which they will assuredly endeavour, as knowing that this War proceedeth from me, and is likely to die with me: and then thou shalt see that this Man is a false Prophet, and I shall have the success which I desire and expect, notwithstanding all his presages.</ns0:note>, and enter into the battel, but put thou on thy robes <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Thy Royal Robes: which thou maist do without any danger, because thou art not the object ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther of the <ns0:hi>Syrians</ns0:hi> rage, or of this false Prophecy.</ns0:note>. And the king of Israel disguised himself, and went into the battel.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 But the king of Syria commanded his thirty and two captains, that had rule over his chariots <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">And the men that fought from them, or with them, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> his whole Army. Possibly the Chariots and the whole Army were distributed into thirty two several parts, and each Captain ruled those Chariots and Soldiers attending upon them, which fell to his share.</ns0:note>, saying, Fight neither with small nor great, save onely with the king of Israel <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">This he ordered, either in Policy, tru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly supposing this to be the best way to put an end to the War: or, with design to take him Prisoner, that thereby he might wipe out the stain of his own Captivity, and reco<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver the honour and advantage which then he lost: or rather, by the Power and Providence of God, which disposeth the hearts of Kings as he pleaseth; and inclined them to this course, that they might, though ignorantly, accomplish his word and counsel.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">32 And it came to pass, when the captains of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat, that they said, Sure<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the king of Israel. And they turned a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />side <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">They drew their Forces from their several quarters to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wards <ns0:hi>Iehoshaphat.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> to fight against him: and Jehoshaphat cried out <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">To the Lord for help, 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 18. 31.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="33">33 And it came to pass, when the captains of the chariots perceived that it <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> not the king of Israel <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Which they easily perceived; either, by their words ut<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tered to God or them; or, by the difference of his shape and countenance from that of <ns0:hi>Ahab,</ns0:hi> which probably many of them very well knew.</ns0:note>, that they turned back from pursuing him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="34">34 And a <ns0:hi>certain</ns0:hi> man drew a bow <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> in his simplicity.</ns0:note> at a ven<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>In his simplicity,</ns0:hi> i. e. ignorantly, without care, or choice, or any design, or thought of reaching <ns0:hi>Ahab.</ns0:hi> Or, <ns0:hi>according to his perfection,</ns0:hi> i. e. with his perfect and utmost strength: which is mentioned as the reason why it pierced through the joynts of his Armour.</ns0:note>, and smote the king of Israel between the <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> joynts and the breast-plate.</ns0:note> joynts of the harness <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Where the several parts of his Armour are joyned together; which possibly were not then joyned with so much art and closeness as now they are.</ns0:note>: wherefore he said un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to the driver of his chariot, Turn thine hand, and carry me out of the host <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Out of the midst of the Host where the heat of the Battel was, into a safer part of the Army. See the next Verse.</ns0:note>, for I am <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> made sick.</ns0:note> wounded.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="35">35 And the battel <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> ascended.</ns0:note> increased <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Grew hot and violent.</ns0:note> that day: and the king was stayed up <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Was supported by Cor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dials, or by his Servants, that by his presence he might en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />courage his Soldiers to Fight more couragiously, and that he might see the event of the Battel.</ns0:note> in his chariot against the Syrians, and died at even, and the blood ran out of the wound, into the <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> bosom.</ns0:note> midst of the chariot.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="36">36 And there went a proclamation throughout the host <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Probably by <ns0:hi>Iehoshaphat</ns0:hi>'s order, with the consent of the chief Captains of <ns0:hi>Israel;</ns0:hi> and possibly with the permissi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on of the King of <ns0:hi>Syria,</ns0:hi> upon notice of <ns0:hi>Ahab</ns0:hi>'s Death, which was the onely thing at which he aimed, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 31.</ns0:note>, about the going down of the sun, say<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, Every man to his city, and every man to his own countrey <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The King is Dead, and the Battel ended: and therefore every man hath liberty to return to his own House and private oc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />casions.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="37">37 ¶ So the king died, and <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> came<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                     </ns0:note> was brought to Samaria, and they buried the king in Samaria.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="38">38 And <ns0:hi>one</ns0:hi> washed the chariot in the pool of Samaria, and the dogs licked up his blood <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Together with the Water wherewith it was mixed.</ns0:note>, and they washed his armour, according <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 21. 19.</ns0:note> unto the word of the LORD, which he spake <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Of which see the Note on <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 21. 19.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="39">39 Now the rest of the acts of Ahab, and all that he did, and the ivory house <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>the house of the tooth</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>teeth,</ns0:hi> to wit, of <ns0:hi>Elephants:</ns0:hi> See <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 10. 18. Not that it was made wholly of solid Ivo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry, but because the other materials were covered, or inter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mixed, or adorned with Ivory. Compare <ns0:hi>Amos</ns0:hi> 3. 15.</ns0:note> which he made, and all the cities that he built, <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> they not writ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ten in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="40">40. So Ahab slept with his fathers, and Ahaziah his son reigned in his stead.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="41">41 ¶ And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Chr. 20. 31.</ns0:note> Jehoshaphat the son of Asa began to reign over Judah in the fourth year of Ahab <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Who Reigned 22 Years: therefore he Reigned about 18 Years with <ns0:hi>Ahab.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> king of Israel.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="42">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:300" />42 Jehoshaphat <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> thirty and five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty and five years <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Part, by himself; and partly, with his Sons whom he took into the Fellowship of his Kingdom. Of which, see more on 2 <ns0:hi>King</ns0:hi> 1. 17.</ns0:note> in Jerusalem: and his mothers name <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> Azubah the daughter of Shilhi.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="43">43 And he walked in all the ways of Asa his father <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">He took the same care for the Government of his Kingdom; and especially, for the Reformation of Religion, that <ns0:hi>Asa</ns0:hi> did: of whom, see <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 15. 11.</ns0:note>, he turned not aside from it, doing <ns0:hi>that which was</ns0:hi> right in the eyes of the LORD: never<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />theless, the high places were not taken away <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Object.</ns0:hi> It is said, <ns0:hi>he did take them away,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 17. 6. <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> He took away those which were Erected to Idols; of which, he seems to speak there, because <ns0:hi>the high places</ns0:hi> are there joyned with <ns0:hi>groves,</ns0:hi> which were generally Erected to <ns0:hi>Idols,</ns0:hi> and not to the True God, as will appear to any one that shall com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pare all the Scriptures where <ns0:hi>groves</ns0:hi> are mentioned; but he could not take away those which were Erected to the True God; of which, this place manifestly speaks; as also that Parallel place, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 15. 14. where see the notes. Or, he took them away, but not fully; or not in the very beginning of his Reign.</ns0:note>; <ns0:hi>for</ns0:hi> the people offered and burnt incense yet in the high places.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="44">44 And Jehoshaphat made peace with the king of Israel <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">With <ns0:hi>Ahab</ns0:hi> first, and then with his Son. This is no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted as a Blemish in his Government, 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 19. 2. and proved of most Mischievous Consequence to <ns0:hi>Iehoshaphat</ns0:hi>'s Posterity; as we shall see 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 9. and 10.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="45">45 Now the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, and his might that he shewed, and how he war<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />red, <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> they not written in the book of the chro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nicles of the kings of Judah <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Whence the most memorable Passages were Translated into that Canonical Book of the <ns0:hi>Chronicles.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="46">46 And the remnant of the Sodomites <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Of whom see <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 23. 17. 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 14. 24. and 15. 12.</ns0:note> which remained in the days of his father Asa, he took out of the land.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="47">47 <ns0:hi>There was</ns0:hi> then no king in Edom: a depu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Sent, and set over them by the Kings of <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> from the time of <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 8. 14. until the days of <ns0:hi>Iehoram,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 21. 8.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> king.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="48">48 Jehoshaphat <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or, had</ns0:hi> ten ships.</ns0:note> made ships <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">As it is expressed, 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 20. 36. Or, there were to <ns0:hi>Iehoshaphat ten ships:</ns0:hi> the Ellipsis of the Verb <ns0:hi>Substantive,</ns0:hi> and of the Praefix <ns0:hi>Lamed,</ns0:hi> being frequent in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Language. Some render the Words, <ns0:hi>he made ten ships;</ns0:hi> so joyning both Texts together, and out of both compleat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the sence.</ns0:note> of Tharshish <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Either, 1. Of the Sea, as this Word is thought sometimes to be used. Or, rather 2. <ns0:hi>To go to Tar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />shish,</ns0:hi> (as it is expressed, 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 20. 36.) and then<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> Ophir,</ns0:hi> as it here follows. See more on 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 10. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> to go to Ophir <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Of which, See 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 9. 28.</ns0:note> for gold: but they went not; for the ships were broken at Ezion-geber <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Which was in <ns0:hi>Edom,</ns0:hi> and consequently in <ns0:hi>Iehoshaphat</ns0:hi>'s Territories.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="49">49 Then said Ahaziah the son of Ahab unto Jehoshaphat, Let my servants go with thy servants in the ships, but Jehoshaphat would not <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Obj.</ns0:hi> It is said, That he did joyn with <ns0:hi>Ahaziah</ns0:hi> herein, 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 20. 35, 36. <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> That was before this time, and before the Ships were broken: for the breaking of the Ships mentioned here, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 48. is noted to be the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> of his Sin, in joyning with <ns0:hi>Ahaziah,</ns0:hi> and of the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> conse<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quent upon it, 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 20 37. And good <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>
                        </ns0:hi> be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing warned and chastised by God for this Sin, <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> not</ns0:hi> be perswaded to repeat it; whereby he shewed the sincerity of his Repentance.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="50">50 ¶ And Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David his father: and Jehoram his son reigned in his stead.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="51">51 ¶ Ahaziah the son of Ahab began to reign over Israel in Samaria the seventeenth year of Je<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hoshaphat <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">By comparing this Verse with <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 41. it appears, that <ns0:hi>Ahaziah</ns0:hi> was made King by his Father, and Reigned in Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />junction with him a year or two before <ns0:hi>Ahab</ns0:hi>'s Death, and as long after it; even as <ns0:hi>Iehoram</ns0:hi> the son of <ns0:hi>Iehoshaphat</ns0:hi> was made King by his Father in his Life-time, as we shall see hereafter; which possibly was done in compliance with <ns0:hi>Ahab</ns0:hi>'s desire upon Marriage of his Daughter to <ns0:hi>Iehosha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phat</ns0:hi>'s Son; and it may be <ns0:hi>Ahab,</ns0:hi> to induce and encourage him to do so, gave him an Example of it, and made his Son his Partner in the Kingdom.</ns0:note> king of Judah, and reigned two years <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Either after his Fathers Death: or one before it, and another after it.</ns0:note> over Israel.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="52">52 And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, and walked in the way of his father, and in the way of his mother, and in the way of Jerobo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />am <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Which Clause seems here added, to shew, how little the Authority and Example of Parents, or Ancestors, is to be valued, where it is opposed to the Will and Word of God.</ns0:note> the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="53">53 For he served Baal, and worshipped him, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">By so <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> and provoked to anger the LORD God of Is<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rael, according to all that his father had done.</ns0:p>
